House in Committee on Bill (No. 148) to amend the Dominion Elections Act, 1900.- Mr. Fitzpatrick.
On section 1,

FITZPATRICK Minister of Justice). This section is intended to amend section 24 of the Dominion Elections Act, 1900, in respect that in so far as the electoral district of Algoma is concerned, the returning officer has the power to fix a date beyond the date fixed for the nomination of candidates and the holding of elections in other countries, if he deems it prudent in his discretion. By the Redistribution Act of last session, Algoma was divided into east and west Algoma, and the effect of the present amendment will be that the returning officer will have power to do with respect to the two ridings of east and west Algoma what he had the power to do with respect to Algoma as it originally stood. It makes the law applicable to the constituency as subdivided. The same thing will apply to British Columbia. There the counties of Burrard, Yale, and Cariboo, have been divided into Comox-Atlin, Kootenay and Yale-Cariboo. The electoral divisions mentioned 243|
in the Act now practically take in the territory covered by the old divisions in British Columbia. That is the only change except that to the list of counties in Ontario in which the returning officer may extend the time for voting we add the district of Nipis-sing, which I am informed is geographically in the same position as Algoma. It is a county covering a great area of country, and some portions of it are unorganized, so that the same conditions that prevail in Algoma apply to Nipissing.

I regard the provisions of this section, as far as a number of these ridings are concerned, as absolutely unjustified. For example, in British Columbia, I have had time to get information about only one of these ridings, but I find that in the riding of Kootenay the provincial elections were held on the same day as in the rest of the province, without the slightest inconvenience, as I am informed. All portions of that riding are reached by rail or steamboat, and I am surprised that the Minister of Justice should present this measure to the House without giving some better reasons for postponing these elections than he has done. The mere fact that this has been done in the past is not of much consequence ; the question is what the conditions are at present. The country has not been standing still, so far as means of communication are concerned, during the last fifteen or twenty years, and in these districts there are better means of communication than there were before. So far as the two other ridings of British Columbia are concerned, I am not in a position to state their condition, but I shall require some good reasons to convince me that the elections should not be held there on the same, day as in the rest of the province. It is not a sufficient reason to state that they are large districts. So far as Algoma and Nipissing in the province of Ontario are concerned, I believe that what I have stated with regard to one of the British Columbia districts is true of one of the Ontario districts -that the provincial election there is held on the same day as the general election.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Which of them ?

I am informed that in the provincial elections the voting in Nipissing is held on the same day as in the other ridings. I am sure the Minister of Justice will regard that as a very cogout reason for carrying out the same policy in this Bill. I am not familiar with the riding of Algoma, but my hon. friend from East Sim-coe (Mr. Bennett) will speak about that. He tells me that there are equally strong reasons why the election there should not be postponed. So far as the ridings in the province of Quebec are concerned. I would not presume to speak of them, not having a knowledge of the facts. The Minister of Justice, I am sure, will be good enough to

make an explanation to the House with regard to these. I am not objecting to this proposal in any case where it is necessary. But I say that there should be very strong, in fact imperative, necessity before any election is postponed. The principle we have followed in this country for more than a quarter of a century is to have all the elections throughout the country held on the same day ; and only for the gravest reasons should that rule be departed from.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: So far as Quebec is concerned, I can speak with some degree of personal knowledge. In the GaspS district there has been absolutely no change within twenty years so far as facilities of communication are concerned. They have not a single railway within the whole district. The facilities for Communication in summer have been somewhat improved, but not to such an extent as to allow the elections to take place under the same condition as in other parts of the province. In Chicoutimi and Saguenay there has been an increase in the facilities of communication. There is a railway which reaches Hake St. John and extends down to the town of Chicoutimi. But it is a very large district and there are many outlying parishes which are in quite an exceptional position. Therefore. I think that the conditions existing in these two districts are such as to justify the action I ask the House to take with regard to them. As to Nipissing, I am personally responsible for having added that district to the number which are treated exceptionally. Looking at the map and taking into consideration the position, I came to the conclusion that the district was not accessible. And, so far as one can judge by looking at the map. it seems to me that this is one of the constituencies which is in an exceptional position. But I am entirely in the hands of the committee so far as Nipissing is concerned. As to the division of Algoma, I merely apply the old law with the verbal changes made necessary by reason of the fact that that territory has been subdivided into east and west Algoma. If there are reasons as to one riding why the old law should not be made applicable, I am quite willing to listen to any objection that may be stated. As to the province of British Columbia, I would ask members from that province to explain the conditions there.

I think it will be agreed that the two ridings of east and west Algoma were formerly the one riding of Algoma. Now, the minister will find upon inquiry, that the government thought it wise and proper to have the elections in the district of Algoma in 1900 on the same day as the general election.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The provincial election ?
L* BORDEN.

No, the Dominion election. The local elections are also held on the same day as in other ridings of the province. Surely, if the election for the whole district as one riding could be held on the same day as the general election in 1900, there is no reason why, now that it is divided, a change should be made. That must appeal to the hon. minister's sense of right.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) I understand, speaks from his certain knowledge when he says that the election in 1900 in Algoma was held on the same day as the general election ?

I am very positive about that from something I recollect-I am con-lident I cannot be mistaken. If a returning officer could do the whole work for these two districts in 1900, and if one candidate ' could look after his interest for the whole district, surely, now that railway communication is improved and there is more accommodation in every way as well as a considerable addition to the number of settlers, the same course could be pursued in two districts with two returning officers and a double organization.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think I will drop it.
Do I understand the hon. minister to say he will drop Nipissing from this section ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
How about Algoma ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I took Algoma because I found it in the statutes we had before. The other statute could not be made applicable to the changed state of things and therefore I included both east and west Algoma in this Bill. If the hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) says that he is in a position, of his own knowledge. to inform the House that the election of 1900 in Algoma was held on the same day

as the general election, of course I shall have to consider it.

I am positive that in 1896, the election in Algoma was held subsequent to the general election, and I am equally positive that in 1900 the election in Algoma was held on the same day as the general election.

The Canadian Northern Railway has been constructed since the last election and runs directly through the western portion of the constituency, taking in Rainy River and all that territory, while the Canadian Pacific runs through the other portion. There is really no necessity for making an exception as to the date of holding the elections there.

I have a communication from a gentleman who is very familiar with that district, in which he says :
In the old days, when It was the custom to hold the Algoma election later than the general election, there was good cause. It was impossible to give the notices required by law within the specified time. But now, it is different. The railway has opened it up and it is now Just as easy to hold the election on the same day as the general election, as it is in any ordinary constituency in the east.

I would call the attention of the Minister of Justice to the fact that, even if there were any reason why the election in Algoma should be held on any other day than that of the general election, the difficulty would arise with regard to Manitoulin Island, which difficulty could only be at some seasons. If any reasons do exist for this provision, they can only apply to one riding and not to two.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In which of the ridings is Manitoulin Island ?
In East Algoma.

With regard to the division of the district of Yale-Cariboo, the leader of the opposition is in error when he says there is no occasion for having the general election at different dates. I may state to my hon. friend, and I know something about the geography of that country, as well as the facilities for travelling through it, that it is a physical impossibility to have the next general election at the same time in what will be the district of Kootenay. There are nine local ridings in which the returning officer will have to act in the Dominion election ; that is to say, he will have to do the actual work of nine returning officers in a provincial election.
Is the hon. gentleman talking about Kootenay or Yale-Cariboo ?

I am talking about Kootenay for the. moment. Now, in the
election of 1900 we endeavoured as much as possible to give every voter an opportunity of voting, and we followed out the practice in the Dominion election of establishing polling places at the same points as in the provincial elections, so as if possible to give every person an opportunity of voting. I may state to my hon. friend that there are sections in that district that cannot be reached by rail or by steamer. For instance, you have all the Fire valley to travel through, you have other parts of the Trail district to travel through, and you have parts of the Lardo where you have to travel by teams, and any person who is acquainted with mountain roads must know that you cannot travel over them in the same space of time as you can country roads. Furthermore, a reference has been made to the election being held at the same time as the general election in what was the old riding of Yale-Cariboo. But the conditions then were absolutely different from what they are now. then all the settlement was in the upper part of the district around Kamloops, and along the railway belt, and there was very little settlement in Kootenay. In fact, I believe that the few people who were residing in Kootenay then did not know there was an election until after it had taken place. That, I believe, is an actual fact. But this was in Mr. Mara's time, before I was elected. That country is settled up now. You must remember that you will have to travel probably 100 miles in one direction in order to deliver the ballot boxes. You cannot cross a range of mountains to reach another valley ; you have to retrace your steps to the central point, and take another direction. Any person who will take the trouble to study the physical features there must come to the conclusion that it is a physical impossibility for any returning officer, within the time between the nomination and election, as fixed by the Act, to do that work.
Why not have two returning officers for each district ?

The Act provides for one for every district. The same remark applies to the Yale-Cariboo district, with equal force. There is no. question, as I stated before, that it is a physical impossibility for the returning officer to do the work within the time.

I would like to put the facts of the case before the leader of the opposition, who seems inclined to take the stand that the Dominion elections will have to be held upon the same day. Tue district of Comox-Atlin is 1,500 miles in length, as the crow flies, from the polling subdivision which will be at Squamish to Surprise Lake. If the election is held in the winter time, you will require a dog train to take up the polling boxes ; if in the summer time, you will require canoes to

take them up. My hon. friend from Yale-Cariboo1 (Mr. Galliher) has said it is a physical impossibility to hold ail election in Kootenay in the time required by law, and it is equally impossible in Comox-Atlin. In fact it is more difficult in Comox-Atlin than in any other district, for the reason that the facilities for travelling are much more difficult. To illustrate by a case in point. On the occasion of the last election the returning onicer went into the then district of Burrard-Comox-Atlin is a little larger than the district of Burrard-and he was obliged to travel five days with a dog team. He had first to travel on snowshoes to break a trail for the dog team to bring the ballot boxes in. It takes him almost fourteen days from the time he leaves. If he takes Nanaimo as the central point of Comox-Atlin. it would be a physical impossibility for him to get into Surprise Camp or to Atlin, as my hon. friend from Victoria (Mr. Earle) can substantiate, in less than fourteen days.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I move that the words ' West riding of Algoma and Nipis-sing ' be dropped from this section.
Is that with the idea of having Eastern Algoma subsequently ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

Eastern Algoma is the most easily approachable, for the reason that a branch line of railway running along the north shore of the Georgian bay runs through a part of the riding, and then it is only a few miles further across to Manitoulin island. In the winter time you can shorten the distance by crossing on the ice. In summer there are numerous boats plying across to Manitoulin. There is a thorough system of telegraph lines all through that district, and a telephone system too, I am informed, on Manitoulin and on the north shore.
Amendment (Mr. Fitzpatrick) agreed to.

As far as the riding of Kootenay is concerned, I am not much impressed by the argument of the hon. member for Yale-Cariboo (Mr. Galliher), who 1 regret to observe has disappeared within the last moment. It is beyond doubt that it comprises nine provincial electoral districts, and an election was held in every one of these nine districts at the recent provincial election. In one of them, Columbia, there was an election by acclamation, in the other eight there were contests. I am informed on the authority of a gentleman whom 1 know very well, and who is absolutely reliable, that there was no inconvenience whatever experienced in holding all these elections on the same day as the elections in the rest of the provinces. The hon. member for Yale-Cariboo dwells on the fact that this district comprises nine provincial electoral districts. The Minister of Justice will re-Mr. MACPHERSON.
member the riding of Alberta. That comprises eight or ten territorial electoral districts. We never found it necessary to postpone that election. We had the whole of the Northwest Territories divided into four electoral districts. We have never found it necessary to postpone the elections in these. Why should there be any necessity for postponing the elections in these districts in British Columbia ? The means of communication in British Columbia are just as good as they are in the Territories. The physical difficulties of crossing the mountains may be greater, but as far as the roads are concerned I do not think there is any great difference between the conditions in those two ridings of British Columbia and the conditions as they were in the Northwest Territories years ago when we held elections at the same time as in other ridings in the Dominion. It seems to me that there should be an irresistible case made out before the elections in any of these ridings should be postponed. Yale-Cariboo is large, Kootenay is large, but so also are the districts in the Northwest Territories ; so are also many districts in Ontario, where the elections are held on the same day as those in the rest of the Dominion. All through the provinces we have conditions of that kind. If you have an active returning officer, and if you empower him to use the means which jnay be at his disposal, I think there should be no difficulty of holding these elections on the same day as in the rest of the country. My hon. friend from Yale-Cariboo (Mr. Galliher) did not say very much about his own riding. He devoted his attention more particularly to Comox-Atlin and Kootenay.
I spoke of Kootenay and I said that my remarks would apply equally well to Y'ale-Cariboo.

I have spoken of Kootenay, and my remarks will also apply to Yale-Cariboo. I do not see why the elections in these ridings should not be held on (the same day as those in the rest of the country and the absence of any special argument in regard to his own riding should be the best reason for believing that the hon. gentleman does not entertain any very strong views upon the subject. I trust the hon. Minister of Justice will not place a blot upon the statute-book by postponing the elections in these ridings unless he is absolutely convinced that it is necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The blot is there unfortunately and we are trying to remove it.

The blot is not there except under certain conditions, whereas, this is a blot under present conditions. May I ask whether the elections in the Chicoutimi and Saguenay district are postponed under the provincial law ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think that if the elections take place in the summer time as

far as Chicoutimi and Saguenay are concerned the voting takes place on the same day. It has taken place on the same day. But if in the winter time I imagine, if there is any justice to be done to the electors, it would be physically impossible to have the election held on the same day as elsewhere, because you have to go all over the riding in sleighs.
How is it in provincial elections ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is the same as in Dominion elections.

Are they postponed in these three ridings ?
(Mr. FITZPATRICK. Yes. My hon. friend of course, understands the geograpi-eal conditions existing in Gaspe. Gaspe is at the extreme eastern end of the peninsula. It is absolutely inaccessible except in summer time by boat and in winter time by sleigh. As far as Chicoutimi and Saguenay are concerned my hon. friend will remember that the district of Chicoutimi and Saguenay takes in the Lake St. John region, the Saguenay river and the whole north shore of the St. Lawrence.

I am quite ready to accept the assurance of my hon. friend as to that, but as far as the east riding of Algoma 'is concerned and as far as these British Columbia constituencies are concerned, particularly Kootenay, I am very strongly of the opinion that they should not be pressed. I would even ask the hon. Minister of Justice to delay for twenty-four hours to make inquiry.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is no objection.
I think he would be satisfied that there is no real necessity for postponing the elections in at least two of them.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I would like at the Aame time to hear all that could be said in favor of the objection that is made to this proposal so that I may be in a position to have all the information obtainable on the subject. I would like to know all that can be said because I must confess that to a large extent I was guided in regard to the east riding of Algoma by what the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) said as to the difficulties of getting access to the island of Manitoulin.

When the distinction was made in respect of the holding of elections in Algoma there was no railway communication at all. This is one of those provisions that was allowed to remain upon the statute-book when it should have been removed. Algoma is just as accessible as many other districts in the province of Ontario. The Canadian Pacific Railway runs along the
north shore of Lake Superior and there is no difficulty in getting to Manitoulin now.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: What about the autumn and spring ?

There is no trouble reaching the Manitoulin island during the period when navigation is opened. After navigation closes there is access from the north shore at Little Current and there is I believe abundant means of communication with eastern Algoma, just as there are with western Algoma. There is no trouble in reaching western Algoma.

In eastern Algoma there are only a few weeks in the spring and fall during which there is any danger connected with reaching the island of Manitoulin; that is in the spring when the ice is breaking up and in the fall when the water is freezing over. That usually takes about two or three weeks. The distance is very short and when the ice is formed there is no difficulty in getting to the island. In the spring of the year up to the time that the ice breaks up it is an easy matter to get to Manitoulin island and when on Manitoulin island the roads will be found to be as good as the ordinary roads of the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Two or three weeks in the spring and autumn might make a very considerable difference. If the elections were held in the spring or the autumn it would make a material difference. My hon. friends opposite must remember that this power is only discretionary with the returning officer. He is not under any obligation to postpone the election. This is only intended to confer upon him the power to exercise his discretion in view of the conditions existing at the time the election is held. Of course, the returning officer would necessarily be a man upon whom we could rely and who would not postpone the elections if there -was not necessity for it.

I perhaps did not make myself clear to the hon. Minister of Justice. I did not urge that there was any reason why there should be a different period for holding the election in East Algoma but what I said was that if there were reasons, and there were at that time, they would apply to both east and west Algoma since they had been divided. The hon. gentleman knows that the Rainy River district which has been made into one riding and east and west Algoma were all contained in the district of Algoma formerly and that if the same reasons existed as formerly for holding the elections on a different day these two ridings of east and west Algoma would not be subject to them now'. But, as my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) points out there is no good reason that would apply to even East Algoma now as compared with any other riding in the province. The hon. Minister of Justice has stated that this

power is discretionary with the returning officer but I want to point out to him, that, notwithstanding the fact that the elections in 1900 were held on the 7th November, at a time when Algoma was perfectly accessible, as much so as in .Tune, the election there was held on a different date. Therefore, the returning officer takes the law as mandatory rather than being a merely discretionary power placed in his hands.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In .Chicoutimi and Saguenay the elections were held on the same day in 1900 as in other districts, because they were practically held in the summer time.

I was in error in saying that in 1900 the election in Agloma was held on the 7th of November ; I find it was held a week subsequently. It would appear to me that the reasons for holding the election in East Algoma on the same day, are stronger than with regard to West Algoma.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My only reason for insisting is because of the Manitoulin islands. Would my hon. friend direct his attention to that ?
The most remote part of the islands is, I think, Little Current, and that is a trifling distance from the main shore ; in fact you can see right across.
In some places it is only 100 yards.

There are little islands in between and the water freezes over early in the fall and the ice remains late in spring, so that it is usual to have uninterrupted communication to every point. The town of Sault Ste. Marie is in East Algoma and the local elections were held in that district on the same day. The Manitoulin islands are one of the most accessible places in Ontario ; and I remember well that the first returns that came in last election were from these ridings.
Mr. GALLI1IER. In view of what the leader of the opposition has further said in regard to Tale-Cariboo and the Kootenay districts, I wish to place the facts before the House. The Kootenay riding is curved out as a subdivision of Yale-Cariboo which I now have the honour to represent, and which after the next election I hope to continue to represent.
Hear, hear.

I shall direct my remarks particularly to the Kootenay, and j they will apply to the new division of Tale- [ Cariboo. I am informed that the leader of the opposition stated that in the nine ridings the provincial election was held on the same day. That is quite true, but the hon. gentleman must see that the one federal returning officer, in. order to establish polling places and to give facilities to the electors to vote, would have to do the same Mr. CLANCY.
amount of travelling as the nine separate returning officers did in the provincial elections.
Is it the practice in British Columbia that the returning officer must travel over the whole riding ?
Yes.

It is not the practice in my province. The returning officer sits in his office in the city of Halifax and makes arangements over the whole constituency, which has many miles of seacoast without any railway, and he never has had any difficulty.
What about the distribution of the ballots between nomination and election.
He sends them out by messengers to his deputy returning officers.

I can only speak of what took place in the Yale-Cariboo election. There is no question, but that it is a physical impossibility for any one man to get over that district in the time unless you give him wings. ' If my hon. friend (Mr. R. L. Borden) knew the district as I do, he would realize that. The returning officer has to appoint his deputies, and swear them in and give his instructions to them personally, and he cannot do that as it can be done in other constituencies. Personally T *would not object to having the election on the same date as the other elections, but I know it is a physical impossibility.
When was the election held last time ?

On the 6th of December, about a month after the general election. I ' am well acquainted with the district and with the means of egress and ingress, and I will be frank with my hon. friend. There are many mining camps where there are fifty or a hundred men who could not vote unless they had a polling place. It is neither fair nor just to ask them to travel from the camp and lose a whole day going to vote. They have an opportunity of voting in the local election, and they should not be deprived of it in the Dominion election. In the matter of settlement and in the matter of places to be reached to establish polling places, the [DOT] conditions are entirely different from what they were ten years ago when every one knnws that the population in the mining camps was very sparse. My hon. friend (Mr. Macpherson) can speak as to the AtUn district, but I know as regards Yale-Cariboo that it is simply a physical impossibility to cover that district in the time provided.

It is most extraordinary that commerce has overcome the difficulties which are spoken of by gentlemen on

the other side of the House. Commercial men have been going through the constituency of Yale-Cariboo regularly, and not [DOT]carrying a bundle of papers either, but ten [DOT]or fifteen heavy trunks.
Mr. G-ADLIHER. On a pullman car.

The whole country is traversed by commerce and it is very hard to make a merchant believe that there is any physical impossibility in getting through that country. The fact of the matter is that we have post offices, telegraph offices, and telephone offices scattered pretty generously through that territory.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If we could only vote by telegraph it would be most convenient.

If the people want to vote they will have no difficulty in voting. The hon. gentleman from Yale-Cariboo (Mr. Gab liher) has told us that one election was over before the people knew there was an [DOT]election at all.
I say so again.

Commerce has shown you how to get through that country and how to get through it regularly. Even in GaspG about which the Minister of Justice speaks so much, the conditions are Wonderfully changed as compared witu fifty or a hundred years ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Brock) has now got me on ground with which I am familiar. In what respect have the conditions changed ?

Ask the Quebec merchant how he deals with that country now as compared with the conditions fifty years ago, and he will ten you that he has his commercial travellers all through the district, and that there are a multiplication of post offices there. Could the returning officer not send the deputy returning officers all the papers by mail, and inform them about the election ? The argument in favour of the principle of having all these elections on the one day. far outweighs any difficulties that might be presented on the other side, and the government should drop this Bill. There may be some injustice done, but that occurs in every act of administration, and the injustice that would be done by holding the elections on the same day is far less than the injustice of making these exceptions which really make it look as if you were providing certain openings for defeated candidates.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That might have been the reason formerly, but we are trying to remedy it now.

The remedy is in the hands of the government because they can fix the elections on any day they like, and they can
give notice sufficiently far in advance to af-ord facilities for voters in these outlying districts. Give the notice a few days earlier, and all the elections can be held on the same day. So far as we on this side of the House are concerned, we are ready for the elections when they may come. But. in view of the failure of the hon. member (Mr. Galli-her) to make out a case for his own constituency. I think the government should drop this Bill, and stand on the principle of uniformity. North of Lake Superior and the Georgian bay at one time we had no post offices, telegraph offices or railroads. This is all changed. Y'ou would be surprised to know that the people up there now read the daily papers. I hope the people out in Cariboo are becoming educated enough to read a weekly paper, at any rate. The hon. gentleman should supply them, and let them know when an election is coming on. But apart from that, the great question in this country is, when we shall have the elections; and the Prime Minister should name the day far enough ahead so that we can have them in the whole country on the same day.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend is evidently quite unaware of the difficulty which we have to deal with. My hon. friend must not imagine that by giving a yeat's notice of the elections we could help the difficulty we are now confronted with. The difficulty is this. There are certain things which have to he done after nomination day : the ballot boxes, the ballot papers, the electoral lists and the instructions have to be distributed. There are only eight days under the law between nomination day and polling day ; and the difficulty arises with respect to those electoral districts in which the physical conditions are such that it is impossible to make the distribution within that time. If my hon. friend's information with respect to Algoma is not more accurate than it is with respect to Gaspfi, then I would not place on his information in this respect that reliance which I generally place on what he says in this House. So far as Gaspe is concerned, suppose the nomination takes place at Perc6, at the ex treme eastern limit of the peninsula, and it is necessary to send the ballot boxes up to Ste. Anne des Monts or Cap Chatte, T. would like my hon. friend to tell me how, after the 1st of December, when navigation is closed, it will be possible to do it in eight days ?
By notifying the men whom you appoint as returning officers in the different istricts to be at the nomination and take their ballot boxes home with them.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If my hon. friend had them there, and provided them with relays of horses at every ten miles, they could not do it in eight days. That is a fact about which there is no doubt. In the

first place, along two-thirds of the coast there are no roads, and yon have to use dogs if you get along at all. On the north shore of the St. Lawrence, in Chicoutimi and Saguenay, you have to go from Tadousac, at the mouth of the Saguenay river, to Blanc Sablon, on the Labrador coast, and how are you going to do it in eight days ? it is a physical impossibility.
If you have a will you can do it.

There is no reason why the nomination should be held at the extreme limit of the constituency. The iaw says it shall be held as near the centre as possible, and three poll clerks may be appointed as well as one to distribute the ballot boxes and the papers. As a matter of fact, in the province of Ontario, the ballot boxes are usually held by the various municipalities, and are not required to be taken from one centre to another. The provincial ballot boxes are used.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That explains many things. We are getting light now. If the ballot boxes are not under the control of the returning officers, but are distributed around, we had better look after them.

That has been the case for years. The ballot boxes in most cases are owned by the municipalities and are not in the possession of the returning officers. Where the municipality cannot furnish the ballot boxes, the returning officer is bound to furnish them. But the rule is that the same ballot boxes are used for provincial, Dominion and municipal elections.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I cannot say anything about what is done in Ontario, because I am not there ; but subsection d of section 41 of the Act requires that ' the returning officer shall deliver to each deputy returning officer, two days at least before the polling day, a blank poll book, forms of oaths to be administered to voters, envelopes, sealing wax and a ballot box.'
Let me tell the hon. gentleman how he does it.
Oh, oh.

Is there anything laughable or absurd about it ? The only thing absurd is the ignorance of the laugh. The election clerk gets the ballot boxes from the clerk of the municipality, and after they are used he returns them to the municipality. They are gathered up and distributed by the election clerks.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is very improper.

There is another point that has been overlooked by our hon. friends opposite, that is, that the ballot papers are not printed until after the official nomination ; and, as a general rule, it takes two Mr. FITZPATRICK.
days to print the ballot papers before they can be given to the returning officer.

In the larger districts the returning officer never attempts to-distribute all the ballot boxes and papers himself. He delegates that power to others, which I think the law permits him to do. Either the election clerk or some other person is employed by the returning officer to make the distribution. In the outlying counties what is to hinder the returning officer employing half a dozen men, if necessary, to-cover the whole ground ? Where there is a will there is a way.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is no difficulty about his employing others if he chooses. His obligation is to deliver to each returning officer the ballots, the lists and the ballot boxes. When the distances are so great that after the ballots are printed he cannot do that within the eight days, what is going to be the result ? If he cannot reach every polling division in the whole district within the eight days, is that not sufficient reason for postponing the election ?
Why should any group of men be deprived of their right to vote ? Is it not fair to say that if the conditions existing at the time the elections are held are such that any important group in the community may be deprived of the right to vote that the returning officer shall have power to postpone the election in order to give these men the right to vote, especially as this provision is restricted to two or three counties in the province ? So far as Ontario is concerned the only district added is East Algoma, and the contention of my hon. friends opposite is that this provision is not necessary for that constituency. I have heard nothing on this side in support of the contention ; nobody on this side seems to be interested in the question of whether the election be held on the same day or on a subsequent day. I shall take into consideration what my hon. friends opposite say, but I want to point out that it is not a case of whether all parts of one island are accessible, but whether all parts of the constituency are accessible. Suppose the elections are held in the autumn or spring there might be difficulty.

Manitoulin island is a very old settled district. Farmers have been living there for years and there is a splendid system of municipal organization. The island is almost connected with the main shore and there will be no difficulty in traversing it at any season of the year.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It there is no difficulty, if the thing can all be done within I the eight days, then I will have to consider the propriety of dropping the provision as

to East Algoma as I did that with regard to the west riding. So far as Quebec is concerned, I know what I am talking about because I have been about the country and know it. All that is necessary is to take a map for instance of the county of Chicoutimi and Saguenay and look at the distance from Tadousac to Blanc Sablon. It must be 150 miles and there is a dog trail for most of the road.

I shall not dispute with my hon. friend about the province of Quebec ; he knows more about it than I do, and I am willing to accept his assurance. In regard to Ontario I find, according to the statutes of 1887 the latest I was able to get in the library, that all the provincial elections took place on the same day, and I understand from Ontario members that the same thing is done under the statutes of 1897. If that is so I am sure the Minister of Justice would recognize that it is not necessary to have this extension.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If that is so there is no reason for our making an exception.

So far as Yale-Cari-boo is concerned, let me say that if the mode of procedure that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Galhher) seems to think should be followed by returning officers were generally adopted about two-thirds of the constituencies in Canada would require to have the elections postponed. He seems to argue that the returning officer himself should go to every deputy returning officer and deliver the boxes and ballots and administer the oath. This is not done. It is not done in my own county, it could not be done in Halifax. If it was done1, Halifax would require to be in the excepted list. We have 100 miles to the east with no railways, and 40 miles to the west with no railways, and it would be a physical impossibility for the returning officer to go over that county and visit every district between nomination and polling. The returning officer sends to some of these polling districts a messenger, and for many other districts he has the deputy come to Halifax and personally receive from him the ballot boxes and ballots. I see no reason why the same procedure should not be followed in the constituencies in British Columbia. How shall we say that any one of these is any more difficult to traverse than one of the great constituencies of the west before they were recently divided.
I do not think I will dispute that.
My hon. friend will not dispute that ? Well, he practically abandons his case.
Oh, no.

Because all we require is that there shall be a deputy returning officer, who by means of messengers or by requiring his deputy returning officer to-come to him shall distribute his ballot boxes and I'allots within the period between nomination day and election day. Why cannot the returning officer use exactly the same polling districts and polling places as those which were established in the recent provincial election ? Ought there to be any difficulty about that ? One would not siippose that if there were any run l desire on the part of the returning officer to accomplish this within the time mentioned that he would have the slightest difficulty in doing so. My hon. friend is very confident about coming back. So far as he is personally concerned I would like to see him here, but perhaps not, from another standpoint.

I do not think I was egotistical enough to speak in that way. I said I hoped that I would have the honour of being returned. I think a man may modestly say that he hopes he will come back to this House.

If he is coming back we would like- to have him back as early as possible and therefore to have the election as early as possible. Of course we will endeavour to console ourselves if he does not. hoping that we might see him occasionally, but if he is to come back we hope we may see him at the earliest possible moment, and therefore there is every reason from his own standpoint why we should

have the election on the same day as they are held In other parts of Canada.
Is not Yale-Cariboo the mining camp where they play poker for 150 votes ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Order, order.

I have no doubt they can play poker In some of the mining camps In Yale-Cariboo.
Mr. oENNETT, The national game.

Yes, the national game. I hope the leader of the opposition does not think that it is not purely from a desire to give to every person and to every part of that district, whether to the miners in the mining camps or to those along the direct line of railway and steamboat which my hon. friend travelled very comfortably, an opportunity to vote that I am taking the position I now take. I certainly want to give every man entitled to vote an opportunity of voting. I therefore want to have every facility granted to these men whether they be working as miners in a mining camp even although it be very remote as some of these camps are. There is no question about the fact that while we are civilized and advanced in British Columbia as far as means of travel are concerned, there are many mining camps in the mountains miles and miles away from these means of transportation, and I want to see these men have ftn opportunity to cast their vote whether they vote for me or against me. The vote is their own privilege and they have a right to vote for whoever they please. Now, it is all very well to say in general terms : We see no reason why this should not be done. Why the elections should not be held here at the same time as the other elections. Personally I have no interest in postponing it. In fact, if you wish to know my personal preference, I would rather face the fight on the day of the general election than later. Rut I am instructed, and I know, that it is a physical impossibility to have this election on the same day as the others. I have stated that two or three times already. I do not know how often this district must be subdivided to bring it down to the same position as other constituencies in regard to holding the elections, but I know that though it has been subdivided, it still covers a vast area. It has been said that there are constituencies of great area in the Northwest. That is true, but the conditions are altogether different. From any point in these constituencies in the Northwest you can strike off to any other point. But you cannot do that in a mountain district. You may travel fifty, a hundred or even two hundred miles in one direction to reach a certain point. From there, you cannot cut across the mountain range to a point that may be only twenty miles away, for there is no means of communication. The only thing Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
you can do is to go back to the starting point and strike off at another angle. I do not know why we should have to repeat these things. They are facts, and facts that anyone knows who has travelled through the mining regions. Many points you can reach comfortably in a parlour car or in the cabin of a nice steamer, travel such as the leader of the opposition, like myself, has frequently indulged in up and down that country. But when you get away from the points reached by these means of communication, the travelling is very different indeed.

I would like to read to my hon. friend a statement that has been sent to me by a gentleman in that district. It differs from the statement of my hon. friend (Mr. Galliher). I do not' know whether my -information is under a misapprehension or not. Probably my hon. friend would say he is :
The Kootenay district according to Representation Act, 1903, section 2 of the British Columbia division of that Act, provides that the electoral district of Kootenay shall comprise the provincial electoral districts of Cranbrook, Columbia. Fernie, Kaslo, Nelson, Revelstoke, Ross-land, Slocau and Ymir. As far as I can see, and all others here agree upon the point, there is no physical reason for postponing the election for this district to any later date than that of the general election. We had a general provincial election in 1903 for the same districts and the election was held in all these districts on the same day. No inconvenience whatever was experienced thereby, and, inasmuch as the Dominion elections will be upon the same lists and with the same polling places, there is absolutely no excuse for making the change. In the Columbia electoral district there was no poll held, inasmuch as the member was elected by acclamation. But an election took place in all the others. Each one of these districts is reached by rail or steamer. The means of communication are good, and in fact the returns were in from every point, with the possible exception of one or two small polls, on the night of the election.	*
If that is a correct statement of the facts, I do not think there is any adequate reason for postponing the election in this district.
Who wrote that letter ?

It is not a confidential letter, and I do not think the gentleman who wrote it would have the slightest objection to my making known his name. It Is from Mr. A. H. MacNeil, K. C., of Rossland, to whom I wrote for information.

There is nothing there except what my hon. friend (Mr. Borden) has repeated. It is stated that every district is reached by rail or steamer. It is true that probably some portion of every district is reached by rail or steamer, but there are points in these districts that cannot be reached in that way. As I said, you have to go by team to the end of the settlement, and from one point you cannot strike across to another even though it is only ten or

fifteen miles away, but must retract your steps and strike off at another angle.
Does my hon. friend agree that the returns from all these districts except one or two were in on the night of the election ?

That is probably true. But my hon. friend (Mr. R. L. Borden) knows that returns can be sent by telephone or telegraph from places which could not be reached by driving except with great expenditure of time.

But, if you have the means of communication by telephone or telegraph, cannot you bring in your deputy returning officer on the day of nomination and send him out with the ballot box ?
Mr. GALLIHER, Of course, you can reach a man by telephone or telegraph if those means of communication exist, but-
I think my hon. friend (Mr. Galliher) is not very much in earnest.

So far as I am personally concerned, I do not care to have the election postponed. But I am told that it is impossible to hold it on the day of the general election, and I know it is impossible.
Progress reported.

Bill (No. 149) to amend the Representation Act of 1903-Mr. Fitzpatrick-was read the second time and House went into committee thereon.
On section 2,
What is the effect of this ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This is to correct a clerical error. When the Bill was prepared last session an Act of the Ontario legislature 1901 was overlooked. It was one of a series of Acts which are passed each year by the legislature of Ontario, entitled ' Acts to amend the Statute Laws.' They are amendments to various statutes and especially this Act in question has reference to the Ontario Territorial Divisions Act, chapter 3, of the Revised Statutes. The amendment consists in shifting the boundary between the provisional judicial districts of Algoma and Thunder Bay, twenty minutes westward from eighty-five degrees west longitude to eighty-five degrees, twenty minutes. The effect of that I canjnot realize myself, but it was in order to make our description of that territorial division agree with the territorial division as described in the local statute.

It would be difficult to tell what the effect really is. The hon. gentleman has no doubt looked into it; is
he prepared to say if it affects the popu* lation

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Territorially it will make a very trifling difference, I could not say how much. Twenty minutes is not much.

It depends upon how fast the hon. gentleman travels.
Mr. FITZPATRICK, I know nothing about it except that the gentleman who is responsible for it in my department, Mr. Fraser, drew my attention to the fact that we had overlooked this Ontario Act of 1901, and told me it was important to make the definition in our Representation Act agree with the territorial description given in the Ontario Act. My hon. friend can take my word for it that there is nothing serious in it.
It is assuming that this description is exactly the same as in the Provincial Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

I was going to suggest that as the government are getting out maps of each constituency it would be desirable if they would prepare a map of these constituencies so that we might examine them before the Bill is finally passed.
On section 1,

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Sections 7 and 8 of the Representation Act slipped into their present position where they are now, by mistake. Hon. gentlemen who may have a copy of the Act will see that in chapter 60 of the Act of last session, sections 7 and 8 form part of the beginning of, the Act and therefore apply to all that comes after it ; that is to say, 7 and 8 will apply to all the schedules for all the provinces because they are at the beginning of the Act. Section 7 says :
The limits of every electoral district bounded by a river extend to the middle of that river.
8. The nearness of an island or islet to an electoral district is measured by the relative distance between either side of the island or islet and the shore of the opposite electoral district.
These two sections are taken from the Quebec Act, Revised Statutes, Quebec, chapter 2, sections 67 and 68. The intention was to put these two sections at the head of the Quebec schedule so that they would apply exclusively to Quebec. There is no reason why they should apply to any other province because the electoral divisions of the other provinces are regulated upon different lines. But so far as Quebec is concerned the limits of the electoral district, where it is bounded by a river, extend out to the middle of the river, which is the boundary ; and when there are islands or

islets in a river separating two electoral districts the island or islet is counted with the electoral district to which it is nearest. There is no reason why these sections should apply to all the provinces, and it may create confusion ; there is every reason why it should apply to Quebec because it is part of our municipal organization.
On! section 3,

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I propose to amend that so it shall read as follows :
(f.) For the purpose of defining the constitution and boundaries of the counties mentioned in paragraph (a) and suh-paragraphs 10, 11, 15 and 16 of paragraph (c), of subsection 3 of section 3 of the Representation Act, chapter 6, of the Revised Statutes, the said paragraph and sub-paragraphs respectively shall be read and construed as if the words ' Section 1 of ' in each of these paragraphs were struck out.
My hon. friend will understand the moaning of this bv examining the statutes of Canada of 1886.
It would take a little while to work it out.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Here is the point. Perhaps my hon. friend will be better able to appreciate it after I have made my explanation. I do not intend to ask that the Bill shall go beyond the committee stage at this sitting. The Representation Act, 1886, chapter 6, of the Revised Statutes, section 3, defines the limits of each electoral district in the province of Quebec. In the province of Quebec the counties of Ottawa, &c.
As they were respectively constituted on the thirty-first of January, one thousand eight hundred and sixty-one, section one of chapter seventy-five, of the Consolidated Statutes for Lower Canada, shall each be an electoral district and shall each return one member.
That is to say that these divisions as constituted under section 1, of the old Revised *Statutes of Lower Canada shall each return one member. Then they go on to describe other counties which they say 'are constituted as they were constituted under section 1 of the old statute. Speaking generally, therefore, all the provisions of the old statute are applicable to all the other counties except these and three or four others, for instance, Quebec county which is my own county as it was Bonstituted on the 31st January, 1861, by section 1 of chapter 75 of the Consolidated statutes for Lower Canada. The same thing applies to LotbiniSre, Bellechasse and Beauce.
I thought they had included all these counties in the first general statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, they included in the first general statement Ottawa, Pontiac,

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Hochelaga, Jacques Cartier, Laval, Vau-dreuil, Soulanges, Laprairie, Chambly, Richelieu, Yamaska, Maskinonge, St. Maurice, Champlain, Montmorency, and others, only a certain number of them. Then they go on and distinguish. I would like to point out the difficulty that results from that. The old statute of Lower Canada, chapter 75, section 1 provides :
The counties, cities and towns hereinafter mentioned, shall be the subdivisions of Lower Canada upon which the representation of the people thereof in the legislature shall be based ; and the said counties are those intended for all purposes in these Consolidated Statutes and in the Consolidated Statutes of Canada, except only where it is otherwise expressly provided, either in the said Consolidated Statutes or in some local or special Act remaining in force and applicable to the subject of the enactment, that is to say :
Then they go on to give a description of the different districts. Then section 2 of the statute provides that:
All augmentations or gores of parishes, townships or seigneuries, and all cities, towns, villages or reserves for the same, not specially mentioned in this Act, shall be considered as forming part of the county in which the principal part of such locality or in the immediate vicinity of which, such city, town, village or reserve is situate, unless it be otherwise ordered by some statute in force, for any purpose or purposes.
Then it goes on :
Wherever both banks of any river in Lower Canada are in any district or county, there the river itself is within such district or county :
2.	Wherever one bank of any river is in one district or county and the opposite bank is in another, there the centre of the main channel of the river is the boundary between the two districts or counties, each of which extends to the centre of such main channel ;
3.	And wherever any river or portion of a river is in the county, it is also within the district of which such county forms part.
All these things are provided for in sections 2 and 3 particularly of the consolidated statutes of Quebec, chapter 75 and are applicable to all the counties except those that are constituted under section 1. The effect of the amendment is that in the province of Quebec, where we have only 65 members and where the number does not change, the counties shall be the same counties as were constituted under the Consolidated Statutes for Lower Canada by section 1, chapter 75.

That results from the provision made in the statute that certain districts settled from time to time shall become part of the counties which they adjoin ? That is exactly the idea. I see that you simply strike out section 1.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes. Sections 7 and 8 are not mentioned, because we constitute the counties under the old Conso-

lidated Statutes for Lower Canada. In view of the fact that In our province we have only 65 constituencies and that they remain the same we retain the old division as we had it previous to confederation.
This is really for the purpose of making the law as we understand it already ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As we understand it now.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 4,
Paragraph 5 of that part of the said schedule which deals with the province of New Brunswick is repealed, and the following paragraphs are substituted therefor :-
' 5. The electoral district of Victoria shall, as heretofore, consist of the counties of Victoria and Madawaska, and shall return one member.
6. Each of the remaining counties of the province shall form an electoral district and shall return one member.'

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
A mistake was made in the New Brunswick schedule, it having been overlooked that the old county of Victoria had been divided by a provincial Act into the two counties of Victoria and Madawaska and that these two counties have since that date formed the electoral district of Victoria, which is entitled to return one member. It will be seen that under the schedule as it now stands there would on account of this mistake appear to be 14 electoral districts in the province each entitled to return one member, whereas the province is only entitled to 13 members.
On section 5,
The said schedule is further amended by adding at the end thereof the following :-
' The Yukon Territory shall form an electoral district, to be called the electoral district of Yukon, and shall return one member.'

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That was omitted.
Bill reported.
I understand that before the Bill is read the third time the bon. minister is to furnish a map of Algoma so as to ascertain whether the limits as described are correct or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: ARBITRATION WITH THE GRAND TRUNK RAILWAY.

speechtext:
Bill (No. 152) respecting an arbitration between His Majesty and the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada (Mr. Fitzpatrick) read the second time and House went into committee thereon.
On section 1,

maintopic: ARBITRATION WITH THE GRAND TRUNK RAILWAY.
speechtext: What are the questions that will arise on this arbitration, and under what circumstances have the disputes arisen ?	*

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: ARBITRATION WITH THE GRAND TRUNK RAILWAY.
speechtext:
In 1879 the government originally purchased that portion of the Grand Trunk Railway extending from Riviere Du Loup, 110 miles below Quebec, to a place called Hadlow on the shores of the St. Lawrence almost opposite the city of Quebec. The road extended at the south side of Levis up to a point called ChaudiSre curve, and then came down again towards the city of Quebec on the south side of the St. Lawrence to Hadlow cove. From Hadlow to a place called South Quebec, there is a piece of line that also belongs to the Grand Trunk Railway, but that piece between Hadlow and Quebec South remained the property of the Grand Trunk Railway. At a subsequent period it was decided to build a branch line extending from St. Charles on the line of the old Grand Trunk purchased in 1879, down to a place called Harlaka Junction, thence from Harlaka Junction on to the town of LGvls, and from the town of Levis to a place called South Quebec. It will be borne in mind that there are two links there from South Quebec to Hadlow, one the property of the Grand Trunk, and the other from Hadlow to Chaudiere Junction, the property of the government. By the original agreement the government granted to the Grand Trunk Railway Company, for the purpose of using its yard at South Quebec, running powers over that portion of the line extending from Hadlow to Chaudiere curve, and on the other hand the Grand Trunk Railway gave to the government the right to use that portion of its line between South Quebec and Hadlow Cove. The government had running powers over the road from South Quebec to Hadlow and the Grand Trunk Railway had running powers from Hadlow up to Chaudiere curve. After the St. Charles branch was built down to Point Levis, then the importance of Harlaka Junction came in. Harlaka Junction is the point where the Quebec Central Railway intersects the Intercolonial Railway, and the Quebec Central, has running powers over the Intercolonial Railway from Harlaka Junction up to L6vis. There is considerable interchange of traffic from the Quebec Central Railway to the Intercolonial Railway. The Quebec Central Railway hand their traffic over at L6vis to the Intercolonial Railway, and the Intercolonial Railway takes the westbound traffic west. Under the original agreement running powers were conferred upon the Intercolonial Railway over this little piece of road belonging to the Grand Trunk Railway between South Quebec and Harlaka Junction, and the Grand Trunk Railway says r We gave you running powers over that, but we did not give it to you for the purpose of taking freight from the Quebec Central Railway ; you must hand that freight over to us at
7G75

South Quebec and we will haul it west, but if you do not you will have to pay us for each car you receive from the Quebec Central that you haul over this little piece belonging to the Grand Trunk. They claim from $2 to $2.50 a car which they charge either to the consignee of the freight or to the Quebec Central. Our argument is that when that freight reaches Point Levis it becomes Intercolonial Railway freight and we have a right to handle it and to get the tolls on it from the time it reaches our line at I.cvis until it gets to its destination. We argue that the parties to the agreement of 1879, had in contemplation not only the freight of the Intercolonial Railway proper, but all freight that was gathered from intersecting lines until it reached the point of destination at Levis. That is the difficulty with respect to the 1879 agreement. There is another trifling matter which arises out of the fact that they are making certain charges for handling our freight at South Quebec which we think are too high. Subsequently, in 1898, when the Drummond County Railway was acquired by the government, another agreement was made between the two companies with respect to the use of the Grand Trunk line from Ste. Rosalie up to St. Lambert Junction, and thence over the bridge into the Bonaventure depot. In return for that, the Grand Trunk were under obligation to hand over to the Intercolonial Railway certain freight that was intended for points eastward. We hold that the Grand Trunk have not carried out the conditions of their agreement in respect of the handing over of this freight at Ste. Rosalie, and as a result difficulties have arisen out of that agreement. All these matters have been referred to arbitration under the conditions of the original contract which provides for arbitration in case of dispute, and it is to carry out the terms of file original agreement that this arbitration was entered into. When the matter got before the arbitrators, we discovered that it would be important to get access to all the documents and all the papers on both sides and the arbitrators found that they were without power to grant the necessary orders for the discovery. It is for the purpose of getting these additional powers and authority to summons witnesses that this Bill is introduced. The arbitrators sajr that they have not got these powers, and' it is at the suggestion of the arbitrators that this legislation is asked for.
At One o'clock, committee took recess.
Committee resumed at Three o'clock.

maintopic: ARBITRATION WITH THE GRAND TRUNK RAILWAY.
speechtext:
I do not rise to oppose this clause of the Bill, but rather to express my regret that the Bill does not go much further and occupy a very much larger field. We have been entering into other agreements with the company referred to in the Mr. FITZPATRICK.
Bill, the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada, with relation to matters of a somewhat similar nature to those that have led to the dispute which is now being arbitrated. It appears that for the last six years, under the contract of 1898, the Grand Trunk Railway Company, in the opinion of the government at all events, have been refusing to the Dominion the traffic which they had agreed to give to the Intercolonial Railway. That has been persisted in so that the government have found it necessary to have an arbitration with the company to dispose of the question. Now, we have during this session been spending week after week in discussing an agreement with the government of Canada and the Grand Trunk Railway Company with relation to traffic matters, and especially with relation to the diversion of traffic from Canadian ports to American ports. I say the Grand Trunk Railway Company, because that is the real party to the contract which we call the Grand Trunk Pacific contract. We have again and again endeavoured to get hon. gentlemen opposite to see the need and propriety of inserting in this agreement carefully prepared provisions to protect the people of Canada as against the self-interest of the other contracting party ; but we have been told over and over again that we were dealing with an honourable company, a company of such a character that we might rely upon it; and the government, instead of inserting proper clauses to protect the people against the selfish interests of the company, knowing all the time that this same company were not carrying out honourably, according to the opinion of the government, a contract which had been entered into six years ago, have refused to accept the amendments proposed by the opposition for the purpose of protecting the people against that company. Under these circumstances I am somewhat surprised that the government should bring in at this session, while the country has still before it the recollection of their attitude with regard to the Grand Trunk Pacific contract, a Bill to enable them to get at the books of the Grand Trunk Railway Company in order to see plainly whether that company told the whole' truth or not with regard to the course the traffic took under that agreement of 1898. Why, Sir, when we proposed jn one of our amendments that the Dominion government should have the right to inspect the books of the Grand Trunk Railway Company with reference to the traffic that is carried from the Northwest to the ocean, the government voted our amendment down, and the hon. gentlemen behind them, in dutiful allegiance to their party, but regardless of the interests of the country, backed up the government in that refusal ; and yet all that time hon. gentlemen opposite knew that the company which they refused to protect the people against, was absolutely, according to their own opinion, refusing to carry out the obli-

gations they had themselves entered into with regard to the traffic. Therefore the introduction of such a Bill as this may be regarded with some surprise. Here we have a Bill enabling the arbitrators to compel the Grand Trunk Company to produce their papers. Why, Sir, when we asked that there should be put into the Grand Trunk Pacific Bill a provision that the Grand Trunk Company should be obliged to disclose its papers to the government, they said, no, we do not require them. They said that, with the knowledge that they were quarrelling with the Grand Trunk Company at that very moment on the same subject, and were getting no redress. Under these circumstances I think we have a right to criticise the attitude of the government on this matter. It is quite true, the hon. gentlemen had settled their agreement with the Grand Trunk Company. That was the only answer we ever received. The Grand Trunk Company could get alterations made in the contract when they needed them, while the government would not ask for the slightest alteration on behalf of the people. When they are introducing this Bill to give the arbitrators greater power, why do they not go a little further ? For the past six years they have had an agreement with the Grand Trunk Company which has not worked satisfactorily. The hon. Minister of Justice tells us that certain traffic which the Grand Trunk had agreed to hand over to the Intercolonial has not gone to the Intercolonial ; and there is a dispute between them as to whether it ought to go to the Intercolonial or to the Grand Trunk. We all know that these questions will arise. On the one hand, the Grand Trunk Company, looking after their own interests and not after the interests of the country, will take every advantage they can to take the traffic over their own rails and on their own trains, and to put the freight charges into their own pockets. Nobody blames the Grand Trunk for that. We only blame the government of the day that allows them to do it, and refuses to put provisions into contracts entered into with the Grand Trunk that would enable the country to get what it ought to get. Now, we propose not only that the government should have the right to inspect the books, papers and vouchers of the Grand Trunk relating to this traffic, but that if there should be found any reason for complaint that the Grand Trunk Company are not carrying out the provisions of that contract with regard to the course or direction of the traffic, that matter should be investigated by the Board of Railway Commissioners, and reported to this parliament for action. The hon. gentlemen not only refuse to give us the power to inspect the papers, or to take upon themselves that power, but they refuse to give the Board of Railway Commissioners the power to investigate and report to this House.
Not one step -would they take to enable the country to get protection against what has been going on apparently for the last six years under the contract of 1898. Therefore I say it is a matter of regret in this committee that this Bill, good as it is, does not go further and provide once for all for all contracts between the government and the Grand Trunk Railway. It should have provided for a full investigation of all matters not only under this contract but under any other railway contract, which they may enter into with that company, and it should have provided that in any arbitration or proceeding, either by arbitration or the Board of Railway Commissioners, they should have all the power for which the government is now coming to parliament to ask under this Bill. For that reason and not because I object to the Bill which is all right so far as it goes ; I say that we ought to go further and when the government have entered into a contract of such enormous interest and value to this country as that respecting the Grand Trunk Pacific which is infinitely greater in its relation to the interests of the country than the comparatively small agreement with which we are now dealing, I say they ought to have applied the knowledge and experience that they have derived in the last six years in their traffic negotiations and dealings with the Grand Trunk to the new contracts that we are entering into. They should have availed themselves of that experience to put every necessary provision in the new contracts instead of voting them dowm ns they did when they were proposed by the opposition.
