I desire to call the attention of the House and the government to the matter of the resignation and treatment of Lieutenant-Colonel Gregory, of the 2nd Dragoons of St. Catharines. Probably the shortest way to bring the matter to the attention of the Minister of Militia would be to read the letter which Colonel Gregory wrote me last month, in which he asked me to give my attention to the matter, as representing the people of the county in which Colonel Gregory has resided since his infancy. I propose therefore, to give Colonel Gregory's own words to the minister and the House in order that they may have a full understanding of the facts. Colonel Gregory, in writing to me, said that his term of command of the 2nd Dragoons was about to expire when the officers of the regiment signed a requisition requesting him to accept an extension of term. Colonel Gregory goes on to say :
I did not make application for an extension, but as I had been requested by some of the officers of the permanent force to accept an extension I called upon the District Officer Commanding, and -told him if my term of command was to be extended I wished to know it, and if it was not I wanted to be relieved of my command at once. I stated that if I accepted an extension at all I wanted it for three years.
Is this the same letter which was published in the [DOT] Mail and Empire ' on the 23rd of June ?

I would not say it is the same. In effect it is, but it is not a verbatim copy. This is a letter addressed by Colonel Gregory to myself, as representing in this House the people of the county in which he resides.

On the 4th of August Colonel Otter wrote me that the period I named would not be entertained by the department. He was quite willing, had that day recommended me for an extension of two years and trusted it would be approved.
I heard nothing more about the matter until on the 2nd of November I saw a copy of the general order of September 3rd, in which my term had been extended to July 12th, 1904.
I immediately sent in my resignation and a few days later received a letter from Colonel Otter saying he had my resignation, but before forwarding it he was writing urging that my term be extended as recommended and not to be surprised at some delay. Shortly after this I was asked to make a report as to the fitness of Major W. R. Ferguson for the position of second in command which he held, and as I was given to understand by Colonel Otter that some one was urging the matter, and believing that Major Ferguson would be gazetted out if he did not resign, I advised him to send me his resignation, which he did, and which I forwarded.
On the 10th of January Colonel Otter wrote me directing me to at once recommend Major Glasgow as regimental major, also for the officer who was to succeed him. I replied that at present and under all circumstances did not feel disposed to accede to his request. Colonel Otter wrote me again January 14th requesting an explanation for writing such a letter, claiming I was in duty bound to do as directed. I replied on the 18th stating that my reasons were that I did not consider it was in the interest of the regiment that he should be promoted at present. On the 21st January I received another letter from Colonel Otter saying, I now tell you it is necessary you should recommend Major Glasgow as second in command, saying further ' You may be sure I have good reasons for asking for this action on your part.' On the 23rd I had an interview with the General Officer Commanding in Ottawa and he gave me to understand that my time of command had been extended for two years or would be extended. On the 25th I called Colonel Otter by telephone and told him if his anxiety for the promotion of Major Glasgow was on my account there was no longer the necessity for it as the General Officer Commanding had informed me on the Saturday previous that my time of command had been extended for two years, and to me Colonel Otter replied that he knew more about the matter than any one else, as he had made the arrangements, and later on in a private interview told me that my extension to two years depended upon, me recommending Major Glasgow, saying further, that when in Ottawa some time previous to this the General Officer Commanding had told him to express to me his regrets that he was unable to carry through my extension for a longer period than one year, and that after saving the General Officer Commanding he went to another.
On the night of the 25th, I had a meeting of the officers of the regiment followed by a dinner to which a number of gentlemen not in the regiment were invited and were present. After the dinner I entered into an arrangement with Major Glasgow that he was to remain in command of his squadron until after this camp in June and in the meantime take a course in the Royal Military College, and I would then recommend him for the position of second in command. The next day I wrote the District Officer Commanding, notifying 2444
him of arrangement with Major Glasgow and that I expected to receive a letter from him concurring in the arrangement, but which' ' I did not get.
At an interview I had with Colonel Otter a few days later he informed me that he had reason to believe that nothing but the recommendation from Major Glasgow would secure my extension as recommended and stated that I would only be playing into the hands of those opposed to me and sacrifice the regiment as well if I resigned as I threatened to do before I would recommend Major Glasgow if he did not take steps to improve his qualifications.
On the 22nd February I wrote the district officer commanding again, reiterating what I was prepared to do, and again on the 29th asking if my letter of the 22nd would be acceptable and if my tenure of command was to be extended beyond the 12th of July, 1904, and received a reply dated March 2nd stating that he had written Major Glasgow a few days before, and that he had promised to attend the school before camp for a course, and that he (Colonel Otter) was quite prepared to forward his recommendation at once, and asking me to forward the recommendation as soon as possible. Again on the 3rd of March Colonel Otter wrote me in reply to my communication of the 29th February stating that the recommendation of Major Glasgow as second in command should be sent in at once and ho had every reason to believe that the extension of my command would follow.
To this I replied on the 7th that if Major Glasgow did attend the school as he had promised he should remain in command of his squadron until afi^er camp, when his promotion would immediately follow, and that I was firmly convinced my proposition was not only reasonable but in the interest of the regiment, and that I had come to the conclusion that if my extension of time demanded upon me acceding to the demands of Major Glasgow, I had better resign my command at once.
On the 10th of March Colonel Otter wrote me that he regretted that I could not see my way to make the recommendation and that as action had shortly to be taken, he now proposed to do it himself. After getting the ' Canada Gazette ' of June 11th, in which appeared the promotion of Major Glasgow to second in command, also that of Captain Sharp to major commanding * D ' squadron, and Lieutenant D. Dell to rank of captain, and none of which I had recommended, I forwarded my resignation to the district officer commanding and asked to be relieved of the command of the regiment at once. My resignation was sent in on the morning of Wednesday, June 15th.
Now, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me, although I am not technically what would be called a military man, that the department has put itself entirely in the wrong. The people of this country have a deep interest in seeing the Militia Department administered in the interests of the militia of Canada. And digressing here for a moment,
I think I can say without any fear of contradiction that it is only as an institution for the benefit of the people of Canada that this militia organization exists; and speaking

as a representative of the people I am just as much entitled to say what I think of it as if I were a military man technically or enrolled in the militia force. I need not of course say that those of us who do not technically belong to the militia force nevertheless have the interest of the militia as much at heart as those who do belong to it ; and it is because we have only so many hours in a day and so many days in the month in which we can work at anything, after getting the necessary sleep that nature requires, that we are not all of us able to take that active part in militia affairs that some of us do and others would like to do. Now the ease of Colonel Gregory seems to me to be a pitiable one, pitiable from the standpoint of the interests of the people of this country, not to qualify it in any stronger language. I ask the House to accept one statement from me without proof, and that is that Colonel Gregory is, as far as a man can be who is not a regular soldier belonging to the regular army, as well qualified an officer, as careful, as earnest, as painstaking, as self-sacrificing in the expenditure of time and energy in the performance of his duty as any militiaman or any other man in the Dominion of Canada possibly could be, and not belong to the regular army. Colonel Gregory has been known up in the county of Lincoln where he was born and has always lived, to have, as some critics of his would say, spent too much time over the militia ; he is known to have sacrificed his money, even his financial interests in his devotion to the welfare of the militia and in the energetic performance of his duties as a militiaman. No man on either side of politics, I am not afraid the most violent Reformer in the county of Lincoln will contradict me in saying, that no man on either side of politics will say that Colouel Gregory as a military man is not absolutely qualified for the performance of his duties, and he has seen that the officers under him and with whom he is associated are also well qualified. It is evidenced by this letter that Colonel Gregory has realized his duty to the country, and to the officers above him as well as to the officers beneath him, and to the whole community in what he was called upon to do. He seemed to think that the duty he was called upon to perform was not a mere bagatelle ; he realized that he. had a serious duty to perform to those in authority over him in the militia, and to the whole people of Canada, in the exercise of the duties that devolved upon him while an officer in command of that troop. Now he was called upon, as is seen by this correspondence, he was invited, as it were, to ask for an extension of time, he was asked if he would accept an extension of time. It does not matter for what length of time ; the point is this, that he was not going to be allowed Mr. LANCASTER.
to have any extension of time unless he did what, Mr. Speaker, unless he certified to a thing that, whether he was right or wrong in his judgment, he would have been a dishonest man if he had certified to holding the opinion he did.
My hon. friend is probably not aw-are that Colonel Gregory had one year's extension of time without any condition, and he does not pretend there was any condition.

Colonel Gregory has had an extension of time of one year before this extension of time without any condition. The question is not whether he should have an extension of time for more than one year. It is idle to say that a different rule or principle should be applied according as the extension of time was long or short, for one year or more. No matter whether it was for one month or three months, for one year, or ten years, or a hundred years, the principle is the same, and it was intimated to him that if he did not do something which he could only do on the assumption that whether it was right or wrong does not matter, and which he could not do as an honest man, he was told that if he did not do it, he could not get that extension. If that principle was to prevail in any department of government it is easy to imagine what the consequences w'ould be. If it was to prevail in the Finance Department, in the Department of *Trade and Commerce, in the Department of Inland Revenue, in the Department of the Postmaster General, in the Department of the Minister of Customs-now I have named the departments of all the cabinet ministers who are in the House except the Minister of Militia. I say that if this principle was to prevail, what confidence would any one have in those departments or in any other institution in which it was allowed to prevail ?
: If Colonel Gregory was wrong in his opinion, that might be a reason for telling him , that he was no longer fit to command, but ' it would be no reason for imposing upon I the people a commanding officer who was ! exercising his functions as he was entitled ' to exercise them, and still telling him that ' he could not remain in command unless he 1 exercised his functions on a different side | of a question to what he in all conscience ' thought he ought to exercise them.
! Sir FREDERICK BORDEN. Would the * hon. gentleman state what was the condi' tion ?
1 Mr. LANCASTER. The condition, accord, ing to this letter, was that if he would re-i commend Major Glasgow- as second in com-1 mand his extension of time would at once t follow. He said he could not do so, because t Major Glasgow was not qualified in his 1 opinion, not having the necessary military

training. He was right in that statement, and was asked to certify the contrary.
He was qualified.

I differ from the hon minister. I am not a military man, bar I can understand facts and inferences, and the results of facts, in regard to the Militia Department as well as I can understand them in regard to any other department. It is quite clear that Major Glasgow at that time was not qualified, because Major Glasgow partly did afterwards what Colonel Gregory was insisting would have to be done at that time before he could be qualified. The hon. minister may be right technically in saying that he is qualified now, but at the time it was sought to obtain Colonel Gregory's recommendation he was not qualified, and I would like the hon. minister to explain why it was that this gentleman had to get a further qualification before he could get the certificate.
If the hon. gentleman will look at the papers which were laid on the table of the House he will see by Colonel Gregory's own report that Major Glasgow was qualified in the summer of 1902.

I differ from the hon. minister. That may be his way of looking at these papers. I must speak of the facts as I understand them. It is all very well for the hon. minister to put his construction on certain things, but I am sorry to say that I cannot find the facts to be as h.; represents them. We must differ in respect to the certificate that Colonel Gregory gave. The fact stands out clear and distinct, and I would not be doing my duty to the people if I did not insist upon this fact being presented clearly to them. The fact stands out clear and distinct that Colonel Otter told him that some one was urging him to secuie the recommendation on behalf of Major Glasgow. As the hon. minister does not seem to understand it, I will read it again :
On the 23rd I had an interview with the General Officer Commanding in Ottawa, and he gave me to understand that my time of command had been extended for two years or would be extended. On the 25th I called Colonel Otter by telephone and told him if his anxiety for the promotion of Major Glasgow was on my account there was no longer the necessity for it, as the General Officer Commanding had informed me on the Saturday previous that my time of command had been extended for two years, and to me Colonel Otter replied that he knew more about the matter than any one else, as he had made the arrangements.
Colonel Otter had made the arrangement. What arrangement ? Colonel Otter had made the arrangement that Colonel Gregory should have an extension of time. There had to be pressure brought upon him to make the arrangement that Major Glasgow was to be placed in command and that notwithstanding the fact that he was not certified to as being qualified.
Lieutenant-Colonel Gregory says that on the 25th he called up Colonel Otter by 'phone, and Colonel Otter told him that he knew more about the matter than any one else, that he had made the arrangement, and later on he told Colonel Gregory that his extension of two years depended upon his recommending Major Glasgow. If Major Glasgow was qualified without a recommendation by Colonel Gregory, why was Colonel Gregory told by Colonel Otter that his own extension for two years depended upon him granting this certificate ? That is the vice and the mischief of this matter. That is where you are striking right at the heart of our militia. Whether Colonel Gregory's judgment was right or not in saying that he would not recommend Major Glasgow when the government said to him : Although according to your judgment it may be wrong, you must do it, and we will not extend your time of command for two years until you do it, they were introducing a system -that means ruin to the militia of this country. It is an unfortunate thing for the people of Canada. Colonel Gregory would not submit to that, because, being a soldier, he was a man. They cast a reflection upon him. and he said in effect. I am a man. I wall not certify what I do not believe. He said :	I
am responsible to Roland W. Gregory and to Roland W. Gregory's own conscience for what I do, and as my superior officers do not say that my judgment was wrong. I consider that it is my duty to resign in order that the people of Canada may clear up the matter and take such means as they see tit to ensure that the government shall not allow this serpent to crawl in and accomplish the disasters that it will accomplish if this course is allowed to prevail, and which undoubtedly would have prevailed if something had not been done to prevent it by putting the facts before the House, as he idid and as I am endeavouring in my humble way to do, I being the representative of the county in which this gentleman resides. He goes on to say :
Colonel Otter replied that he knew more about the matter than any one else, as he had made the arrangements, and later on in a private interview told me that my extension to two years depended upon me recommending Major Glasgow, saying further, that when in Ottawa some time previous to this the General Officer Commanding had told him to express to me his regrets that he was unable to carry through my extension for a longer period than one year, and that after leaving the General Officer Commanding he went to another person (but did not give name)

I think the House will be curious to know who that was.
-and arranged with him that if I recommended Major Glasgow for the position of second in command my time of command would be extended two years. ,

I do not notice in the correspondence that the hon. minister has referred to a few moments ago any instructions or memoranda by which we can draw any satisfactory inference as to how that result was brought about. There is nothing in the correspondence to indicate how the change took place. There was a changing of mind here on the part of those in authority over Colonel Gregory, but I do not find anything in the correspondence that shows how it came about There should be some explanation given to the House as to how it arose, because Colonel Gregory says that Colonel Otter, after leaving the General Officer Commanding, went to another person, but did not give the name, and arranged with him that if Colonel Gregory recommended Major Glasgow for the position of second in command Colonel Gregory's time of command would be extended two years, and that information had been conveyed to the General Officer Commanding that his time was to be extended for another year. I want to point out to this House, in endeavouring to do my duty in this matter in the interests of the people of Canada, that, although I am not, as I said, a qualified military man, I do understand the difference between a combatant and a non-combatant. I think we all understand without being in the militia that a man who is trained as a surgeon is not the best man to command in a fight. If it is a question of which wing of the army you shall put forward, if it is a question of drill, if it is a question of whether you shall march or counter-march, a surgeon is not the best man to put in command. I want to tell the hon. minister that we have two officers in our district, Major Stull and Major Birch, who, although residents of my constituency, are not both supporters of mine in politics. The hon. minister need not be afraid of that. He has already heard of Major Birch. He knows that Major Birch had a brother who lost his life in South Africa, he knows that he lives in the county of Lincoln, and he knows that he is a well qualified major of these dragoons.
Major Stull is also a well qualified combatant officer in this regiment ; these two gentlemen are the next best qualified after Colonel Gregory to take command of that troop of dragoons. Colonel Otter, who went out of his way to recommend Major Glasgow, for some strange reason, has shown by his course the necessity for having Colonel Gregory's certificate and not that of some outsider who apparently did not know there were two majors who were the next best qualified to command the troop after Colonel Gregory. But what did they do ? Major Glasgow was a surgeon-major ; he took this very much hurried course-I think it was for less than a month-to qualify him, [DOT]and he was appointed instead of Major Stull and Major Birch who were overlooked entirely by whoever was interfering-for somebody was interfering-and this Major
Glasgow who was promoted
I know my hon. friend (Mr. Lancaster) does not wish to mislead the House, but he must know, if he has acquainted himself with the case at all, that Major Glasgow was the next in order of seniority,

I do not know what this government, or this Minister of Militia, means by next in order of seniority, but if he means that Major Glasgow was the next best qualified I take issue with him. Major Glasgow was a surgeon-major

I am sorry to interrupt my hon. friend. The hon. gentleman must know that Major Glasgow was the senior major in command of the senior squadron of that regiment and that he had been in that position for at least two years.
If so, he was there without proper qualification as a combatant officer.
Which is not true.
I am perhaps on dangerous ground not being a militia man-
If the hon. member will allow me
Oh.
I have as much right to interrupt as the Minister of Militia, and I object to the impertinence of the Minister of Inland Revenue in calling ' Hear, hear.'
If I chose to give the floor temporarily to my hon. friend (Mr. Sam. Hughes) I suppose I could do so ?
I hold in my hand the militia list, and I find that these three officers were gazetted on exactly the same day, viz., the 16th of February, 1902.

And I think that list describes Major Glasgow as a surgeon-major. Although not a military man myself I have still impudence enough-if you like to use the word-to believe that a surgeon-major is not so well fitted to command a regiment as a major who is a combatant officer. The fact that he is a surgeon-major merely means that he is given the rank and perquisites of a major, but he is not in the force as a combatant officer. If as surgeon-major, he was two years in command of the troop, then there is another grievance against the government, and I can well understand that Colonel Gregory thought it *was time to put an end to such a state of things. Although as I have said, I am not in the militia, I represent the militia of the county of Lincoln, and I believe it is my duty to raise this question in parliament. As there are other gentlemen on both sides of the House who are well versed in military matters, and who will no doubt take

part in this debate, I shall not trespass further on the time of the House.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Lancaster) has pinned his faith entirely in this discussion on a letter written to him by Lieutenant-Colonel Gregory. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Lancaster) has shown an utter disregard,-I think I might say contempt- for the papers which have been laid on the table of the House, and whenever he was pressed to give fair play to Major Glasgow he shielded himself behind the fact that he has no particular knowledge of military affairs. I would venture to advise the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lancaster) to acquaint himself somewhat with the ordinary rules governing military proceedings and promotions before he attempts to discuss a question of this kind in parliament. The letter which the hon. gentleman read is almost word for word the statement which Colonel Gregory published in the ' Mail and Empire ' on the 23rd of June last ; and before proceeding with the main statement which I have to make on this subject, I will make a passing reference to this statement, which, by the way, I may observe at the outset, was an exceedingly improper statement for Lieutenant-Colonel Gregory to make. It was a direct violation of the regulations of the Militia Department of Canada, and a direct violation of the King's regulations as well ; a fact which must have been known at the time to Lieutenant-Colonel Gregory.
How is that ?
If the hon. gentleman wishes information I will endeavour to give it to him.
At the time Colonel Gregory wrote the letter was he under orders ?
At the time Lieutenant-Colonel Gregory made the statement he was still commanding officer of the 2nd Hussars though possibly under suspension.
Was he in camp ?
Is the minister quite sure that Colonel Gregory was in camp when that letter appeared in the ' Mail and Empire ?
I believe so.
My impression is that he was not.
He was still in command of the regiment.
He had sent in his resignation; he had left the camp and had gone home before he gave the interview.
He is still on the reserve list of officers and is equally under the regulations.
What is the date ?

[DOT] The 23rd is the day it is published. The article in the ' Mail and Empire ' is dated Niagara-on-the-Lake, June 22, from which I assume that the statement was made there and sent from there, and that he was in camp at the time.
With regard to the language of this statement there are just two or three observations which I wish to make. In view of tile statement that unjust conditions are attempted to be made, I wish to call attention to the fact that Lt.-Col. Gregory insisted on having three years' extension, which is the maximum permitted under the regulations, and at the outset refused to accept any less, and threatened to resign his commission if less than three years were given. He finally modified that to two years. Further on he says that he * was given to understand by Col. Otter that some one was urging the matter,' and so on ; the insinuation all through being that either the minister himself was taking a personal interest in this matter, or that some one behind the minister was urging the minister to take this personal interest.
Hear, hear.

Although the hon. gentleman did not make that statement, I make it for him, and I say that such an insinuation is absolutely unfounded and without the slightest justification. Moreover, the hon. member bases his argument entirely upon the ipse dixit of Lt.-CoI. Gregory, and reiterates Col. Gregory's statement as to conversations which took place between Col. Otter and himself, in which Col. Gregory puts words into the mouth of Col. Otter for which there is no proof whatever, and which I doubt very much Col. Otter ever uttered. He says, for instance :
On the 23rd I had an interview with the General Officer Commanding in Ottawa, and he gave

me to understand that my tenure of command had been extended for two years.
I do not believe a word of that. I do not see how it is possible that the General Officer Commanding could have given such an assurance as that when the matter had not been discussed with me, and had not been recommended to the minister. Then he goes on to say that Col. Otter visited Ottawa, and saw the General Officer Commanding and then ' went to another person,' meaning, I suppose, the minister. I wish to say here most emphatically that so far a* I know and believe and can remember, Col. Otter nev'er discussed the question of Lt.-Col. Gregory with me, here or anywhere else in his life.
1 do not know that I need refer to any more of the points mentioned in that letter. But, Sir, I propose, in the discussion of this matter, to refer to the papers which have been laid upon the table of the House. Before doing so, however, let me refer again to a matter which I referred to in a debate which took place in this House on the 23rd of June, namely, the question of the limitation of the extension of Lt.-Col. Gregory's extension to one year instead of three years. There was a recommendation, which will be found in these papers, from Col. Otter that Col. Gregory's term should be extended for two years. That recommendation came before me, and I saw fit-and I believe I acted wisely, as the events prove-to change that to an extension for one year. I did it in conformity with a practice whjich I had adopted; because great injury and injustice may be done to worthy junior officers by these long extensions of time. If after an extension of one year it turns out that there is still good reason why a further extension should be made, it is always possible to make a further extension. No possible harm can be done by limiting the extension in the first place to one year, because it can always be extended another year and yet another year; but the greatest harm and injustice to worthy, capable and qualified young officers may be done by an immediate extension of time to three years at the outset.
Now, to come to the papers. We are told that Lt.-Col. Gregory is a good officer. I do not quarrel with that statement. I believe he is an excellent cavalry officer ; but I cannot say as much for the methods by which he proposed to keep himself in the command of his regiment after the term for which he was appointed had expired. He was appointed for the regular term of five years, and at the end of five years he proposed, by hook or by crook, to continue in the command for three years more, and threatened the district officer commanding that if he did not give him the extra three years he would resign the command of his regiment. Well, Sir, let me point out to the House the peculiar methods which Sir F. W. BORDEN.
this gentleman adopted in order to attain his end. Let me point out the peculiar little game this gentleman was playing. The second in command of his regiment- will the House believe it ?-was a doctor- not Dr. Glasgow, but one of the best friends the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lancaster) has in his constituency or in the neighbouring constituency-Dr. Ferguson, a prominent Conservative. I suppose it is all right for a medical man to hold a combatant position under such circumstances.
With a combatant's rank.

Dr. Ferguson was second in command, with precisely the same qualification that Dr. Glasgow had. Let me stop here for a moment to say, in justice to my profession, that we are sometimes able to fight, and that some of the best combatant officers to-day are medical men. Let me point to Dr. King, whom the hon. gentleman knows. Will the hon. gentleman undertake to sneer at Dr. King because he is a medical man ? I think he will not dare to do it.
Will my hon. friend permit me ? I did not object to his being a medical man. I said he had a medical training only, not a combatant's training.

Which is not fair, if it were parliamentary, I would say it is not true ; because the hon. gentleman knows, or ought to know, if he examined the papers, that Dr. Glasgow possessed exactly as good a qualification as Dr. Ferguson or Dr. King. In saying that I speak of what I know. It does not do for the hon. gentleman to shake his head and make denials against facts. So much for this doctor, the Dr. Ferguson who is all right and to whom the hon. gentleman took no exception. Dr. Ferguson, in accordance with the peculiar methods which I am going to expose on the part of Col. Gregory, was unfit, as I shall show by Col. Otter's report for five long years to fill the position of second in command. He was kept there by Col. Gregory for the very purpose of giving him an excuse for asking that his own tenure of command be extended because the second in command was unfit to fill his place.
Mr. LANCASTER, There is no evidence of that.
The papers will show that.

I will explain. The reason is that Colonel Gregory had made up his mind that for some reason or other best known to himself, Major Glasgow should not be promoted to the position of second in command although qualified, and he insisted that before he would recommend Major Glasgow, although Major Glasgow was qualified, he must have a promise from Glasgow that he would attend another course. For wrhat purpose ? To improve his qualification, not to get qualified, those are not the words.
Oh, oh.
My hon. friend may laugh, but it was to improve his qualification, and those are the words which Lieut.-Colonel Gregory has carefully used.

I am not making any suggestion to the contrary, but I am risking for information. Why is it in this case that Colonel Otter concurs in that and advises Major Glasgow to do it ? He is not in a conspiracy with Colonel Gregory.

Because Colonel Otter was anxious to have peace in this regiment and I dare say Colonel Otter recognized even Colonel Gregory himself would not suffer by taking a further course to improve his qualifications, and he was quite willing to co-operate with Colonel Gregory to insist so far as he could although the officer was qualified that he should take or so advise that he should take a further . course to improve his qualifications which [DOT]were already sufficient technically at any rate for the purpose of promotion.
Now, I wish to come to a little closer quarters with Colonel Gregory and I wish to point direct to the attention of the House to a letter which appears in this file of papers, which was laid on the table of the House. The letter is one addressed by Colonel Gregory, in December, 1902. to the District Officer Commanding, Colonel Otter, with reference to officers of his regiment who he said were * indifferent '. This is a report which refers to those officers only who are * indifferent This is the letter.
Sir, I have the honour to report that the officers mentioned in my report as indifferent are :
,1st. Major Glasgow, who intends taking another course at the school.
2nd. Captain M. S. Muir, who is a poor horseman.
3rd. E. D. Taylor, who is not yet qualified.
Evidently the other two were qualified.
I have the honour to be, Sir,
Your obedient servant,
ROLAND W. GREGORY, Lieutenant-Colonel Commanding 2nd Dragoon*.
Now, I have here the report in detail, the confidential report of Colonel Gregory, dated December 3, 1902, in which he reports upon every officer in his regiment in detail under the headings.
General ability, general professional requirement, practical proficiency in drill and in the field, professional zeal, smartness in performance of duties, horsemanship, capacity for command, judgment, tact, temper, self-reliance, and 1 is he fit for promotion for higher rank ? '
Now, let us look at these men. First, there is Lieutenant-Colonel Roland IV. Gregory himself, who is reported upon by Colonel Otter.
Next comes this Doctor, Major Ferguson, William R. Ferguson, and next comes the other Doctor, the objectionable Doctor, S. H. Glasgow. I follow these two names through under the above headings and I find that whereas Dr. Ferguson, second in command is reported upon as fair, Dr. Glasgow is reported upon in the same column us good. Under the next column where Dr. Ferguson is reported as fair, Dr. Glasgow is reported as good. So it goes on. In nearly every column in this report, Dr. Ferguson is reported, upon as fair, and Dr. Glasgow is reported upon as good. In only one case is Dr. Ferguson reported upon as good where Dr. Glasgow' is reported upon as fair. This I think is somewhat significant. But it so happens that both are reported upon under the heading of ' Practical proficiency in drill and in the field,' as indifferent. But it does so happen too that under the column
Is he fit for promotion to higher rank ?
Mark you they are majors now.
Is he fit for promotion to higher rank ?
The answer to the question by Lieutenant-Colonel Gregory, confirmed by Colonel Otter is * Yes.'
Does that mean that he is qualified, that they reported him qua-fied ?
Qualified for major and fit to be promoted to a higher rank, namely, lieutenant-colonel.
I believe that confidential report also gives the qualifications of officers, does it not 1
No. I read all that it gives, but I will give the qualifications before I have finished.

The hon. gentleman has referred to that qualification which was possessed by Major Glasgow and I would lie glad if the minister before leaving the question of qualification would give exactly the qualifications which these two officers possess.

They both possess the qualification of field officers' qualifications. Ferguson's qualification is R.S.C. and Glasgow's qualification is field officer's which is equivalent as I shall show before I get through with my statement.
Now I want to call attention particularly -because I am dealing with Gregory, the

gentleman who has obtruded himself upon the consideration of this House and this country-to the fact that Colonel Gregory has written a letter which singles out Major Glasgow as being indifferent when the record, his own record, shows that Major Glasgow's qualification and his character for fitness and good conduct are better than that of Major Ferguson, and I wish to show you, Mr. Speaker, that this was part of a scheme to discredit Major Glasgow and to keep on Major Ferguson who was not able to attend drill in 1901, indeed was not in camp at all, was only in camp a few days in 1902 and was not able to go to camp in 1903. There again the game was to keep Ferguson on in order to be able to say that he was unfit. He was unable to speak above a whisper and he was kept in that place as a sort of warming pan so that Colonel Gregory could use him and be able to say : There is no second in command able to take my place ; therefore I must be kept where I am.
The letter to which the hon. gentleman refers accompanies that same report, does it not ? They are of the same date.
This report is not in the letter of Colonel Gregory at all.

The hon. gentleman has read a letter in which Major Glasgow is described as one of the officers who are indifferent. It is dated the 13th of December, 1902, and he gave that same date as the date of this confidential report.
Yes.
Then the letter accompanied the report.

Exactly. And the letter is a misleading one intended to call attention to Major Glasgow in an unfavourable way, while passing over Major Ferguson who was in a worse position, on Lieutenant-Colonel Gregory's own report, than Major Glasgow himself. The hon. gentleman has referred to a round-robin signed by all the officers of Lieutenant-Colonel Gregory's regiment, asking that his term of command be extended. If the hon. gentleman will look through the papers, he will find that both Colonel Otter and Lieutenant-Colonel Gregory were severely reprimanded, I might almost say-it did not amount to that-but at any rate exception was taken to the fact that a round-robin had been signed in that way, because that is absolutely against all military rules and regulations ; and I am informed-I do not state it as a fact-but from all I can hear and see, and reading between the lines, I am disposed to believe that the statement which has been made to me, namely, that Lieutenant-Colonel Gregory procured the signing of that round-robin. This is the Sir F. W. BORDEN.
memorandum that was sent from headquarters :
Will you please inform Lieutenant-Colonel Gregory to communicate to the officers of his regiment that it is highly improper for them to send any communication with reference to his tenure of command.
How could an officer refuse ? This paper is put before him. He does not wish to run the risk of getting the ill will of his commanding officer and he signs it, and such a request is against all military regulations and rules, and the reason is obvious.
It was your duty when you received this round-robin, to communicate to the officers of the 2nd Dragoons the great breach of military etiquette and military procedure of which they were guilty, and to have returned the round-robin to those who signed it.
Now we come to the extension of time. On the 4th of September, 1903, under the heading of ' Appointments, promotions, &c., general order 149 ' we find the following :-
2nd Dragoons-the period of the tenure of command of Lieutenant-Colonel R. W. Gregory is extended to the 12th July, 1904.
It will be remembered that Lieutenant-Colonel Gregory in his letter appears to complain of the fact that he found that Major Ferguson's case was being inquired into and it appeared probable that Major Ferguson would have to resign. Major Ferguson was being kept, as I have stated, for a certain purpose, and later on somebody seems to have ascertained the fact. Colonel Gregory, I believe, feared a medical board to examine into the case of Major Ferguson would follow ; and Major Ferguson was advised by him that he would lose his position and that he had better make a virtue of necessity and resign rather than have any examination.
Who ordered the medical board ?
I did not say that a medical board was ordered. I said that it was expected that a medical examination would be made and a medical board appointed to look into the matter.
Is there any evidence of that in the report ? I do not know of any private correspondence or evidence of that.
I am not aware that there is any.
On what does the minister base his statement.
Whose statement is that ?

I am quoting the paragraph itself. Now Colonel Otter states distinctly in his letter here that there was no question whatever about Major Glasgow's qualification. But we are told that there was an attempt made to make a bargain with Lieutenant-Colonel Gregory, that conditions were imposed. I want to call your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the fact that the man who wished to impose
conditions was Lieutenant-Colonel Gregory himself. First, he wished to impose the condition that his extension must be for three years, and if it was not for ,three years, he forsooth, would have none of it, and would resign his commission-which he thought better of afterwards. But, Mr. Speaker, let me point out the fact that no conditions were being forced upon Colonel Gregory, so far as I know, but he was attempting to insist upon conditions with Colonel Otter before he would agree to do what it was his bounden duty to do, to recommend, unless there was some strong objection against it, the promotion of Major iGlasgow who was next in seniority. And what were the conditions which he wished to impose ? He wished to impose the condition that although Major Glasgow might be promoted to the position of second in command, he should not take that position, but should remain in command, I think it was of D squadron, until after the next camp, that is that he might in name only be second in command ; and that as long as Lieutenant-Colonel Gregory, who has followed him with the utmost hostility and endeavoured to block his .promotion, remained there, he should not act upon the staff and take his position of second in command alongside of the pretentious Lieutenant-Colonel Gregory. When we talk about conditions, those were the terms which Lieutenant-Colonel Gregory undertook to impose upon the District Officer Commanding, Colonel Otter, and Colonel Otter very properly refused to be dictated to in any such way. It is stated that Colonel Lessard went to Lieutenant-Colonel Gregory and asked him to sign the recommendation, and that Lieutenant-Colonel Gregory agreed to do so, and then putting the pen to one side, refused; and after writing letter after letter and doing everything that mortal man could do both Colonel Otter and Colonel Lessard found that it was necessary, in order to do simple justice to Major Glasgow, for them to act without the recommendation of Colonel Gregory, and this they did. I am sure that any impartial man who will read the papers and observe the course which Lieutenant-Colonel Gregory has pursued from the beginning, the means by which he was keeping an unqualified man for fivp years, knowing him to be unqualified, a man who was not able to attend camp in three years, a man who is described in the manner which I will read in a moment, by the District Officer Commanding, Colonel Otter, keeping that man in a position which was directly against the interests of the militia and of the country, in order to keep Major Glasgow down and to keep himself in
I presume the minister means unqualified, not in a military sense ?
Yes.
He does not mean that jViajor Ferguson had not proper certificates.
No, he had no voice.
That is what I want made clear.
I do not know what that would be called.
Had he the same qualification as Major Glasgow ?

I am informed in the department that it is precisely the same, although the letters are not the same. In the case of Major Ferguson it is R. S. I., but in the case of Major Glasgow it is F.O., field oflicer, which is a more recent qualification, but I am informed is just as good a qualification. Now I want to read what Colonel Otter says with reference to this matter. Here is what Colonel Otter, writing to the adjutant-general, says with reference to Dr. Ferguson, second in command :
Toronto, 8th July, 1904.
Sir,-In reply to your memorandum of yesterday's date I have the honour to report upon the duty performed by Major Ferguson, late -2nd Dragoons, during the latter part of his connection with the regiment.
1901,	absent with leave for the whole period of training.
1902,	absent with leave for four days of training.
1903,	absent with leave for the whole period of training.
As to the ability of this officer to perform his military duties satisfactorily I have no hesitation in affirming that owing to the loss of his voice from an affection of the throat he has not been fit for his military duties during the last five years of his connection with this regiment. In this assertion I am sure that both Colonel Lessard, inspector of cavalry, and his own commanding officer, Lieutenant-Colonel Gregory, will bear me out. In the interest of the regiment I should have reported his case long ago, but as he informed me, whenever the inquiry was made, that he hoped soon to be quite well again, I deferred action until it became apparent that his recovery was most doubtful, and that the efficiency of the regiment was becoming affected through the want of a second in command who was able to undertake the duties of that appointment.
I have the honour to be, sir,
Your obedient servant,
W. D. OTTER, Colonel.
Wliat is the date of that letter V

That letter is dated 8th of July, 1904, a few days ago. I do not know that i need go further in the matter. It seems to me it has been abundantly proved that the course which I pursued in limiting the extension of the com-Mr. SAM. HUGHES.
mand of Colonel Gregory, was in the interest of the public service. There is proof that Lieutenant-Colonel Gregory, although he may be a very good officer, was a man who possessed so little regard for the public interest in connection with his regiment that he kept as second in command, for a period of years during which this man was unable to attend camp, a man whom he knew could never be able to succeed him as commanding officer of the regiment.
I believe that the papers justify me in saying that he did it with malice prepense, that he did it deliberately for the purpose of keeping the place warm for himself so that he could hold it for the extra three years or for a longer period if possible. I say that Lieutenant-Colonel Gregory, knowing the facts concerning Major Fqrgusonr, has fallen far short of performing his duty in reference to that officer. I say that he has slrown a malevolent disposition, at least an unfair disposition towards Major Glasgow who was qualified, who has been qualified for three years past and who holds as good a qualification as Major Gregory does himself, by standing persistently in that officer's way and refusing when he had no good reason for doing so to recommend that that officer be promoted to be second in command and before he would agree to sign the recommendation for promotion endeavouring to Impose the condition that Major Glasgow, although he could be promoted to the second in command, should not be promoted and should not eujoy the results of that promotion until after the next camp and until after Major Gregory had passed out of the regiment.
What was the date of the qualification of Major Glasgow for F.O. -Field Officer ?

The date of qualification was the 6th February, 1902. In conclusion let me repeat, if I may, what I have said before, that I believe it is in the interest of the militia and therefore in the interest of the public that these extensions of command should be reduced to a minimum and that no extension of command should be made unless absolutely necessary. I believe it is the duty of the department, and of the head of the deartment to give special attention to matters of this kind and see that abuses such as those which existed in connection with this regiment are not permitted to exist and are not repeated in the service of the militia.

Mr. Speaker, when the hon. minister rose to his feet he reproved my hon. friend the legal member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) for having shown a disregard and contempt for the papers laid on the table of the House. He demanded fair play for Major Glasgow and he said that my hon. friend had shielded

himself behind his lack of knowledge of the duties of a militia officer, at the same time advising my hon. friend to make himself acquainted with the rules governing the militia. A very strange doctrine, Mr. Speaker, coming from the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence, who, as is evidenced by the facts that have been brought before us in recent weeks, has shown an utter disregard and contempt for the papers laid on the table of the House. My hon. friend from Lincoln, I venture to say, and I am within the judgment of the House, adhered more closely to the papers laid upon the table of the House than did the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence. The hon. minister has paid no attention whatever either directly or indirectly to the papers laid on the table of the House except in so far as it suited his own convenience to draw from them improper inferences in relation to Major Ferguson and in relation to the conduct of Lieutenant-Colonel Gregory. A point at the outset and it is an old point of contention between the hon. minister and myself ; he asserted that this letter which Lieutenant-Colonel Gregory wrote to the Toronto 'Mail and Empire' on the 23rd June, was written in direct violation of the King's regulations. I asked him at the time how it was a violation of the King's regulations and he gave us to understand, although he qualified it somewhat later, that Colonel Gregory was then in camp. I am going to show that the hon. minister paid no attention to the papers he has in his hand, because if he had done so he would have found that it was by his own order that Lieutenant-Colonel Gregory was suspended from his command and that he returned to his home dismissed from his regiment on the 20th June, three days before he wrote that letter.
Does my hon. friend think that it makes any difference ?
I am coming to that in a moment. I am merely pointing out to the hon, minister that he was wrong and that my hon. friend from Lincoln did not utterly disregard the papers laid on the table.
That paper is not on the table of the House.
Well, the papers are here in my hands.
Oh, yes.

Furnished by the hon. minister, I presume they are genuine. And here let me ask the hon. minister if all the papers have been brought down. If they have not been we want them. I understood from Lieutenant-Colonel Gregory and other sources that the papers are not all here.

In regard to that, the hon. leader of the opposition
(Mr. R. L. Borden) asked the other day for some letters which had passed between us and Lieutenant-Colonel Gregory. I intended to state before and I shall repeat now what I said to the hon. leader of the opposition to-day that these papers will be here to-night or to-morrow morning. I propose to lay them on the table.

It is four weeks since I particularly specified that I desired these papers as well as the others. I would have thought that with a reasonable amount of effort they might have been here a fortnight ago. Let me point out that if the copy with which I have been furnished of the papers laid on the table of the House is correct, the document referred to by my hon. friend (Mr. Sam. Hughes) is among the papers brought down.
I thought my hon. friend from North Victoria (Mr. Hughes) referred to Colonel Gregory's letter published in the ' Mail and Empire.'

No. I was referring to the minister's letter dismissing Lieutenant-Colonel Gregory. As to the papers which have not been brought down the hon. minister will be able to bring them down possibly after six o'clock in case they are not now here. The hon. minister himself in a former debate referred to the tact that he assumed the responsibility of order -ing that LieutenantHColonel Gregory should not get an extension of command. I do not find any such order here. The hon. minister will remember distinctly that he himself ' assumed the responsibility of issuing the order that Lieutenant-Colonel Gregory should , not get an extension of command. I find no such order here. Will the hon. minister bring that down ?

There is no such order but what happened was that . when the 1 Gazette ' was made out a recom-' irendation was made for two years and that 1 recommendation was modified to one year.
; That is what happened and there were no | papers in connection with it.

The hon. min-[DOT] ister has referred to various. other matters in connection with this subject, and I shall , take up the point in reference to the King's ! regulations. I have shown that Lieutenant-Colonel Gregory was not in camp at the time he wrote that letter to the Toronto i [DOT] Mail and Empire.' Now I want to tell the : lion, miuister one thing so that he will cor:	rectly understand one of the principles of
liberty and of responsible government, and '7 so that he will understand what it is to live . in a free country and not be under the ty-r ranny of some dark age tyrant; I want to tell him that when Lieutenant-Colonel Gre-1 gory is not on duty and is not in uniform he i can write as many letters as he can get the

papers to publish and that he is absolutely independent of the Minister of Militia. Is it a repetition of the Ponton case that the hon. minister would have brought before us ? Is he going to dragoon every man in the militia who dares to stand up before him or the Militia Department ; and endeavour to silence him in this way '!

I would venture to suggest that as a matter of fair play, it would possibly be just as well not to discuss the Ponton case, as my opportunity for speaking is exhausted. I will be quite prepared to discuss the Ponton case when the time comes, but it would be unfair to discuss it at this moment unless I am given an opportunity to reply.

We will discuss the case the minister has before him where the members of the musketry school down here are marched up like so many school boys and ordered to give a statement. The minister talks about round-robins, but what was done in the case of the men attending the musketry school ? Let me ask him how any of these poor fellows down at the school of musketry dare refuse the order of the commandant of the school to say that everything was satisfactory Why should not a lot of free men speak out and say that they wanted Colonel Gregory to remain as commanding officer ? I am glad that last night the men and the officers at the school of musketry showed themselves free men, and ready to stand up in defiance of the tyranny of their superiors, and to take part in the grand demonstration on the departure of the late General Officer Commanding. What are the facts of the case ? Colonel Gregory was in command of his regiment and there was no question as to his qualification. He comes from a military family ; he has been in the force for a generation you may say, and he has always borne the reputation of being one of the best officers in the service. Colonel Gregory had as senior major, one Major Ferguson who was an excellent officer in many ways, but whose voice had failed him. The doctors reported again and again that it was only going to be a temporary failure of the voice, and Major Gregory was absolutely justified in keeping Major Ferguson second in command until some other officer qualified. Any one who has commanded one of these corps knows the difficulty there was eight or nine years ago when an officer had to go to a permanent school and put on all the fuss and feathers of a parade before Her Majesty ; one can readily understand how lots of these fellows hesitated about the expense of going to these schools. Colonel Gregory was justified in keeping Major Ferguson there until some one was qualified for second in command.
What Glasgow had done on the 6th of February, 1902.

I will come to that later on. Colonel Gregory became officer commanding on the 12th July, 1898, and Major Ferguson succeeded to his majority on the 20th of January, 1899, and proved himself to be a very excellent officer. Gregory's five years were up and he was given a year's extension which brought his term to the 12th of July, 1904. I remember distinctly that Colonel Gregory some years ago told me that his business affairs would not permit of his taking hold of the regiment under the proposed reorganization, unless he were given a three years extension. He is a commercial traveller ; is away from home a good deal of the time and he wanted three years in order that he might have a chance under the new arrangement to do justice to himself and his regiment. That is why Colonel Gregory wanted three years extension, and in all fairness he was as entitled to it as any man in Canada was ever entitled to an extension of time. I know for a fact that Colonel Gregory dogged Ferguson to get the best medical treatment possible to have his voice restored so that when he retired from command of the regiment Major Ferguson would be able to take his place. About the beginning of last year we began to see signs of political meddling. Colonel Otter and Colonel Gregory were in Ottawa as is shown by references in the correspondence.
It is simply a statement of Colonel Gregory that Colonel Otter told him, and it is absolutely unsupported.
The minister will not deny that on the 4th of April, 1903, Colonel Otter wrote recommending the extension of Colonel Gregory's command for two years in addition to the other.
Not in addition to the other.

Well for two years. Colonel Otter wrote :
My reasons for such recommendation are these :
1st. The officer next in command, Major Ferguson, is not at present prepared to accept the command, as will be seen by the accompanying telegram in answer to a communication from me as to his wishes in the matter. The remaining officers of the regiment have also expressed their desire in the form of the inclosed petition-
Round-robin.

Call it what you like. They had an absolute right to sign this and the minister cannot lay his finger on anything in the King's regulations or the Army Act to the contrary. The minister must remember that the militia of Canada are not a permanent force paid for 365 days in the year ; but must remember that

we are determined to preserve our individuality as citizens in this free country, and we are not going to be held under the beck and nod of every pettifogging officer no matter how high he may be ; even the minister himself. He must remember that we are not going to be dragooned and held to the strict letter of regulations which do not apply in England to the militia volunteers or yeomanry but only to the regular forces. Does the minister imagine that we are going to allow him to dragoon us into line in this country ? We are not.

Oh, well, we know you are a great man, but I might point out that there are special regulations that apply to the militia in England which are quite as strong as the regulation I read. I am not sure that this particular regulation does not apply to the militia in England, but I think it does, and be that as it may the King's regulations apply to the militia in Canada.
In this country the King's regulations apply only when a man is on duty or in uniform, and the minister knows that because he and I have discussed it on many an occasion.
Oh, well

The minister admits it, and the West York market gardener need not interfere. The next statement of Colonel Otter is this :
The remaining officers of the regiment have also expressed their desire in the form of the inclosed petition, that Lieutenant-Colonel Gregory should remain for another term.
The minister says that the other officers were anxious to get Colonel Gregory out, but I know several of them and I know they are independent free men who would scorn to sign this petition at the request of Colonel Gregory or any one else, if they did not believe it. Colonel Otter goes on to say :
2. That none of the squadron commanders have had charge of their squadrons for more than eighteen months, and lack the experience to fit them to command the regiment.
And I extended the time for one year so that they would have eighteen months, plus a year.
How does the minister get over the statement that Colonel Otter says they were not fit to command ?
After the time was extended a year they would have two and a half years then.

I am speaking of the facts at the time the two years were refused. I have given the reason why Colonel Gregory wished the two years extension and I am now giving the recommendation of Colonel Otter. So the minister cannot turn it on Colonel Gregory and Major
Ferguson and endeavour to show that it was a conspiracy on their part. I am going by the record laid on the table of this House.
Third, That in view of the great improvement in the efficiency of the regiment that has taken place during Lieutenant-Colonel Gregory's command, I think he as deserving of the recognition of his services which I now recommend.
What further proof do we want, in the face of Colonel Otter's own recommendation, of the political meddling of the hon. member for Welland and the senator representing that district ? Mr. Speaker, I agree with my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) that the question asked by his colleague (Mr. Osier) was one of the most important questions that could be asked in this House and I have merely risen to say that although the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Frederick Borden) now declines to answer that most important and very proper question he practically answered this afternoon. It will be remembered that this afternoon a letter was read by my hon. friend from North Victoria (Mr. Hughes) bearing date the 23rd June at which

date it was stated by the lion. Minister of Militia the writer of that letter, Colonel Gregory, was in camp. As a matter of fact he was not in camp and the attention of the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence having been called to this fact that not only was Lieutenant-Colonel Gregory not in camp at the time but that he had been actually suspended by the order of the minister himself some three days before the minister quietly added : I do not know that it makes any difference. Every member of this House knows, every militiamen in this country knows that if Lieutenant-Colonel Gregory had been in camp wearing his uniform on the 23rd of June it would have "been improper for him to have written that letter to the newspapers. Nobody would question that ; but when the hon. minister states that he did not know it made any [DOT]difference whether Lieutenant-Colonel Gregory wrote that letter not merely after he had ceased to be a member of the militia but after he had been suspended by the hon. minister himself, it would seem to be such a monstrous doctrine that I, an ordinary layman would not have believed my ears had not precisely the same theory "been carried into effect in my own city of Belleville. One of our colonels retired after be had served his time in the regiment and when he was on the retired list, happening to make some observations at a private dinner which were obnoxious to the hon. minister, he was called upon to give an account of his words. The answer was sent by the colonel to the minister with the request that it be laid before the General Officer Commanding and while at the same time courteously answering the letter raising the point whether or not the minister had any control over him now that he was on the retired list, no answer was given by the department and although the colonel has written again and again asking that his questions shall be answered he has been unable to obtain even the courtesy of a reply. I think in view of these two facts, the treatment of Lieutenant-Colonel Gregory and the treatment of Lieutenant-Colonel Ponton, which is an actual fact in the history of the militia force, we do not require any statement from the hon. minister as to what his view is as to his rights or intentions in regard to the militia force. I would like to point out to the hon. minister that while he says that the question before the House is a moot question, that the regulations are there and that every one can read them for himself, everybody knows perfectly well that if it is a moot question it could be made a plain question in two minutes by the hon. minister, and if he is willing to have an Act of this parliament passed declaring that no official of the department has any control over an officer who is not on duty every officer will feel himself free and independent if he is not on duty. The doctrine laid down by the hon. minister Mr. NORTHRUP.
brings it down to this that every officer and soldier in the militia, no matter how high or how humble he may be, when he joins the force pledges himself for ever to abstain from politics in so far as supporting the party of the opposition in this House is concerned. But, when it comes to gentlemen in the militia supporting hon. gentlemen opposite it is apparent that they can sign any sort of a document they choose to give a certificate of character to hon. gentlemen opposite and the government does not deem it to be a violation of the King's regulations. But, let any gentleman in the force, no matter what his position in the country may be, express a difference of opinion with hon. gentlemen opposite and he is at once disciplined by his superiors. If that is not a case of dragooning I would like to know what it is.

You will remember that last year I made a protest against any money being expended on the old work and that I pointed out that if the government desired to accommodate the people of that part of the country they would build an entirely new work.

The work is there, it is a government work and the government felt they ought to maintain it. Therefore the engineers recommended that this sum be expended for the purpose of maintaining the old work.

Before I came to parliament last year a meeting of the people of the locality was held and they sent a memorial to the government asking that no more money be spent on the old work but that a new work be commenced some 100 yards away from the old work because the old work was in an improper situation and would never be of any more benefit. That is the old game of bluff. Strike it out if you dare. I dare you to strike it out.
I move that the item be dropped.

I think perhaps on consideration the minister will realize that he had made a mistake. He wants to throw the responsibility upon the hon. member (Mr. Hackett). I know nothing about the transaction nor as to whether it is a wise'expenditure or an unwise expenditure, but I understand the protest of the hon. member (Mr. Hackett) to be that the money was not being spent in the proper place. If the minister had listened to the suggestion of the hon. member, he would have allowed the item to be passed with the intention J that if that were not the proper place to spend the money it would be spent in some adjacent location where people of that section of the country approved of it, or the minister himself or his engineers might think it better to expend the money. I have no desire to increase the expenditure of the country or to ask the minister to allow the item to go through beyond the fact that 1 think it unfair to throw the responsibility of dropping the item upon the hon. member, simply because he made the suggestion that it would be better to spend the money at a place where the people would get greater advantage from it.	.

At the end of every session gentlemen opposite are in the habit of criticising the general expenditure without mentioning a single item to which they object. matter looked into, but it is not a thing that can be decided at a moment's notice to-night. As I understand, the hon. member (Mr. Hackett) asked that the item should be struck out, and I shall be glad to have the engineer at the first opportunity inquire into the necessity for a new work.

The people of that section of the country are not in favour of expending any more money on the old work. I have had a great deal of experience in connection with this work. At every election, local or federal, this work has been taken up, and a certain amount of money put in the estimates for it. Macdonald and Moffatt are good contractors. They entered into a contract with 246	'
the government to construct this work, and a large amount of money was voted for it. Why was It stopped ?

Harbours and rivers, Ontario-Amherstburg -dredging, $30,000.
Will that complete the work ?

This work is practically rendered necessary owing to the increased draught of boats that are now going up and down the river. The approaches to the

wharfs would only permit a boat drawing sixteen feet to come up to them. This item is put in the estimates with the intention of calling for tenders to perform work so as to increase the depth of the water and permit larger boats coming into the wharf.
Ontario-Barry's Bay, Madawaska river, wharf, $4,500.
Explain this.
The estimate was $4,500 ; there has been no expenditure ; it is intended to prepare plans and call for tenders.
What do you mean when yon say it is a departmental matter.

I mean that the resident engineer reports to the chief engineer that a certain amount of money is required for repairs, and when the report comes to the minister it is scrutinized and a vote asked in accordance with the departmental report.
Ontario-Braeebridge wharf, $5,800.
What is the total cost, and has the contract been let ?

$7,000 is the estimated cost; the contract is not yet let.
Ontario-Burlington channel pier, $20,000.

What is the explanation of this ?
Mr. n l .uAN. This is under contract; it is a revote to complete the payment.
